docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The cyber-security landscape is constantly evolving. While major operating systems like Windows, Linux, and Android receive frequent updates to address critical vulnerabilities, malware creators continuously devise innovative methods to infect as many systems as possible. This challenge is compounded by the diverse nature of today’s digital ecosystem. From high-performance servers to embedded systems, the wide variety of hardware architectures makes it difficult to establish a unified approach to combat malicious software effectively.

At its core, malware refers to any piece of code specifically designed to compromise the (CIA) triad—Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability—of a system without the user’s consent. While early forms of malware were limited to simple viruses that could be easily removed, the modern malware landscape has evolved into a complex array of threats, including ransomware, trojans, botnets, and rootkits. Modern malware payloads are characterised by their sophisticated evasion techniques. They employ advanced methods such as polymorphism and environmental awareness to remain undetected during inspections, only revealing their true nature under certain conditions. Additionally, recent malware often uses legitimate packers to disguise its harmful intent. This shift from static files to advanced and adaptive execution processes has created a detection gap that traditional methods struggle to address, leading to a need for intelligent, AI-based detection techniques.

Table of Recent Impactful Malware AttacksSource

Incident Year Primary Threat Main Consequence Change Healthcare 2024 BlackCat Ransomware National healthcare payment paralysis; $2B+ loss. Heathrow and European Airport Disruption 2025 Ransomware Shutdown of airport operations across Europe, including major functions like check-in and boarding at Heathrow. Phishing Campaign against Ukrainain armed forces 2024 Infostealer Usage of malware tools to steal credentials from messaging platforms and internal systems, exposing secrets related to military operations. Snowflake Data Break 2025 Infostealer Exposed employee credentials, which were later used to break Snowflake’s cloud platform. Affected over 100 major organisations, including AT&T, Ticketmaster and Santander Bank.

docs.title: Traditional Malware Detection Methods
docs.text:
Various software applications use different algorithmic methods to identify malware in a system. The three primary methods for detecting malware are behavioural analysis, signature-based detection and heuristic analysis. A brief overview of each method is specified below.

  • Behavioural method - This method focuses on monitoring the behaviour of programs in real time in a controlled and safe environment. Instead of relying on known malware signatures, behavioural analysis observes how a file interacts with a system. If a program displays suspicious behaviour—such as attempting to access unauthorised files or established processes—it can be flagged and quarantined. This approach is particularly effective at identifying new or unknown malware variants that do not have established signatures.
  • Signature-based method - This is one of the commonly used techniques to detect malware, where a database containing signatures of known malware are stored and tested against software to establish whether it is a malware or not.
  • Heuristic-based method - Heuristic-based malware detection uses expert-defined rules, anomaly patterns and lightweight machine learning models. This method tries to generalise from previously observed malware behaviour and code characteristics.

docs.title: Why Traditional Sophisticated Signature-Based Method fails?
docs.text:
As the cybersecurity landscape undergoes continuous evolution, modern malware has increasingly adopted sophisticated techniques to circumvent traditional malware detection methodologies. Several illustrative examples are presented below: -

  • Polymorphic malware, exemplified by variants such as Emotet, Zeus, and TrickBot, demonstrates the capability to incessantly mutate its binary representation each time it is accessed or downloaded. This dynamic behaviour effectively enables these malicious entities to evade conventional signature-based malware detection mechanisms, posing significant challenges to defensive measures.
  • Contemporary malware exhibits a heightened awareness of its operating environment and employs advanced sandbox-evasion techniques to circumvent defensive measures. This includes the detection of virtualized environments and the implementation of execution delays, thereby masquerading as dormant.
  • Fileless malware that operates solely in memory and utilise legitimate system utilities poses a significant challenge to heuristic-based detectors, which predominantly rely on static malicious patterns and predefined rule sets.

These limitations highlight the weakness of modern, rule-based detection mechanisms against adaptive and sophisticated malware, motivating the shift towards data-driven, machine learning based malware detection system.

docs.title: AI Based Malware Detection Methodology
docs.text: In the recent years, focus on malware detection techniques has shifted from simple machine learning (Random Forest, SVM) to Deep Learning and Graph-Based approaches. Recent approaches model malware as structured program representations such as Control Flow Graphs (CFGs), rather than treating binaries as flat byte sequences. Ma et al. (2019) proposed a detection framework that leverages CFGs to extract deep semantic information from Android applications, achieving a high detection precision of 98.98% after the experiments were conducted on 10010 benign applications and 10683 malicious applications. Recent survey work by Grebehans et al (2025) identifies GAN as a primary tool for detecting and modelling adversarial threats in a dynamic environment. Unlike static analysis, dynamic GAN analyze API calls, system call traces and network connections. Retraining the defensive systems with synthetic adversarial threats renders detection stronger.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8629067
  2. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=10830491

docs.title: Dataset Taxonomy
docs.text:
To systematically understand the landscape of datasets used in research related to malware detection, we group them into three categories based on the tpye of analysis:

  1. Static Analysis Datasets – datasets derived without executing the malware (analyzing binaries, headers, permissions, sequences).
  2. Dynamic Analysis Datasets – datasets generated by executing malware in controlled environments to collect behavioral traces (API/system calls, sandbox logs, network activity).
  3. Hybrid Datasets – datasets that combine both static features and dynamic behavior for richer representations.

Each category plays a distinct role in machine learning-based malware detection, with trade-offs in feature complexity, computational cost, and resilience to evasive techniques.

docs.title: Static Analysis Datasets
docs.text:
Static analysis datasets remain widely used in both classical machine learning and modern deep learning research because they enable faster feature extraction without needing the execution of the binary.*These datasets often include extracted features (PE header, byte sequences, disassembly opcodes, permissions) suitable for both traditional machine learning models and neural networks.

Key static malware datasets used in research:

  • EMBER 2018 – A large benchmark with feature vectors extracted from Windows PE files. It contains benign, malicious,and unknown samples and has beenxtensively used to evaluate ML classifiers.
  • EMBER2024 – A newer, larger version supporting multiple file formats and additional classification tasks those including malware detection, family classification,behavior identification.
  • SOREL‑20M – A very large PE corpus of around 20 million samples with feature vector, widely used to push ML scalability.
  • BODMAS Dataset – A mid-scale PE dataset including raw binaries and extracted features with detailed malware family labels; often considered more balanced and recent than EMBER.
  • PE Malware Machine Learning Dataset: Public corpus with raw labeled PE binaries (~200 K+) that enables direct binary-level learning.
  • Other static benchmarks include Drebin-derived Android sets, MalImg image-based representations, and MalGenome for Android malware research.

Static features commonly used

  • PE headers, metadata (imports/exports).
  • Byte histograms and n-grams.
  • Opcode sequences or disassembly features.
  • Android APK permissions and intents.

Static datasets often support binary detection and family classification tasks and are amenable to both traditional ML (e.g., LightGBM, Random Forest) and deep models like CNNs on byte sequences.

docs.title: 2.2 Dynamic Analysis Datasets
docs.text:
Dynamic datasets arise from executing malware in isolated environments (e.g., Cuckoo/CAPE sandbox) and capturing behavioral artifacts such as API call traces, system calls, filesystem activity, and network traffic. These datasets better reflect runtime behavior and can detect evasive techniques that aren’t apparent when using static methods.

Prominent dynamic datasets include:

  • MalBehavD-V1 – A dataset of API call sequences obtained by executing Windows executables in sandbox environments.
  • Avast-CTU Public CAPE Dataset – Combines sandbox logs capturing rich behavioral traces suitable for ML tasks.
  • Cuckoo JSON Behavioral Reports – Community-shared dynamic logs (API calls, file activities) often used in behavior-centric ML research.
  • Dynamic Android Datasets (e.g., from CICMalDroid with dynamic logs) – These include runtime sequences and sometimes network traces.

Dynamic datasets tend to be smaller due to the cost of execution and collection but provide richer sequential features suitable for recurrent networks or temporal models.

docs.title: 2.3 Hybrid and Large-Scale Multimodal Datasets
docs.text:
Hybrid datasets combine static and dynamic aspects to capture a fuller representation of malware behavior, often required for robust detection.

  • Avast dynamic + static combined corpora – Some research has produced datasets that mix static feature extraction with behavior logs for family classification tasks.
  • MH-1M Android Malware Dataset – A recently released large collection with APK metadata and rich extracted attributes spanning many years, enabling studies on temporal drift and multi-feature learning.
  • Longitudinal Datasets (e.g., LAMDA) – Temporal Android benchmarks used to study concept drift, combining static features and longitudinal labeling across years.

docs.title: 2.4 Dataset Characteristics and Use-Cases
docs.text:
Dataset Year Approx. Size Type Label Source Typical Use Cases EMBER 2018 2018 ~1M feature vectors Static VT + internal labels Binary detection, ML benchmarks EMBER2024 2025 ~3.2M+ Static VT + challenge set Malware detection, family & behavior classification SOREL-20M 2020 ~20M Static Internal + telemetry Large-scale deep learning BODMAS 2020 ~134K Static VT + curated labels Balanced dataset, family studies MalBehavD-V1 2021 ~2.5K Dynamic VT + sandbox Behavioral sequence models Avast-CAPE 2022 ~50K+ Dynamic/Hybrid Sandbox traces Behavior analysis LAMDA 2025 ~1M+ Static/Temporal VT + temporal splits Concept drift studies MH-1M APKs 2025 ~1.3M Static-rich AndroZoo + VT Android multi-feature models

In conclusion, Static datasets (EMBER, SOREL-20M, BODMAS) are the most widely used in malware detection research due to scalable feature vectors and benchmarking tradition. Dynamic datasets (MalBehavD, CAPE) are less common but critical for behavior-oriented detection models. Hybrid/Longitudinal sets (LAMDA, MH-1M) reflect the field’s push toward multidimensional representations and temporal robustness. Dataset choice strongly influences model design. Static models favor gradient boosting and CNNs on embedded features, while dynamic/hybrid approaches lean on sequence learning and graph-based representations.

docs.title: EMBER
docs.text: EMBER was released by Endgame in 2018, EMBER (Endgame Malware Benchmark for Research) became the de-facto benchmark for static Windows PE malware detection using machine learning.

docs.title: Number of Samples
docs.text:
• ~1.1 million PE files total
  • ~900K labeled (train)
  • ~200K unlabeled (test/holdout style)
  • Roughly balanced benign vs malicious in labeled portion (~50/50, but not perfectly)

The dataset includes raw feature vectors instead of raw binaries and pre-extracted static features.

docs.title: Feature Extraction Method
docs.text:
EMBER uses handcrafted static PE features, extracted without execution:

Feature categories include PE header metadata (machine type, timestamp, section count), section information (names, entropy, sizes), imported/exported functions, data directories, byte histogram, byte-entropy histogram, string information, general file statistics with a total of dimensionality around 2,381 features.

docs.title: Label Source
docs.text:
Labels are derived from VirusTotal detections.

Typical labeling heuristic:

  • Malicious: detected by ≥ X AV engines (commonly 5+)
  • Benign: detected by 0 engines
  • Ambiguous: excluded or marked unlabeled

docs.title: Class Imbalance
docs.text: The official train split has approximately an equal amount of benign and malicious samples balanced, however, the family distribution is highly skewed. Moreover, packed malware is disproportionately represented and the real world imbalance that is required is not reflected. This ends up making EMBER more of a research based dataset than a realistic deployment dataset.

docs.title: Time Splits
docs.text: One of EMBER’s strengths is that it contains timestamp metadata. This is a consequence of the original paper that proposed chronological evaluation. however, many follow-up papers used random splits instead of temporal splits, causing leakage.

docs.title: Weaknesses
docs.text:
Since the dataset doesn’t contain raw binaries, limitations are reached when trying deep byte-level modeling. There is also the added noise that comes from VirusTotal. It is limited by concept drift and can be used for statc analysis only. Handcrafted feature bias and Feature leakage risk coz of the timestamp feaature.

The EMBER dataset also includes temporal metadata that enables chronological evaluation of malware detection models. Each sample contains an “appeared” timestamp indicating the month in which the executable was first observed in the wild. This temporal labeling allows researchers to simulate realistic deployment scenarios in which models are trained on earlier malware samples and evaluated on later ones. Such evaluation protocols are important because malware evolves rapidly and can cause distribution shifts in feature space over time (Anderson & Roth, 2018; Galen & Steele, 2020). The availability of timestamp information therefore makes EMBER suitable not only for benchmarking classifiers but also for studying temporal robustness and concept drift in malware detection systems (Galen & Steele, 2020).

docs.title: References:
docs.text:
Anderson, H. S., & Roth, P. (2018). EMBER: An Open Dataset for Training Static PE Malware Machine Learning Models.

Galen, T., & Steele, J. (2020). Evaluating Performance Maintenance and Deterioration Over Time of Machine Learning-based Malware Detection Models on the EMBER PE Dataset.

docs.title: Classical Machine Learning (2018–2020)
docs.text:
The dataset EMBER 2018 was introduced by Hyrum S. Anderson and Phil Roth in the paper EMBER: An Open Dataset for Training Static PE Malware Machine Learning Models (2018). The dataset contains approximately 1.1 million Windows Portable Executable (PE) samples, represented using feature vectors derived from static analysis of binary metadata (Anderson & Roth, 2018). These features include header information, imported functions, section statistics, byte entropy distributions, and string-based characteristics extracted from the executable structure.

In their original evaluation, Anderson and Roth demonstrated that gradient-boosted decision tree models implemented using LightGBM achieved extremely strong detection performance on the dataset. Their baseline classifier achieved a ROC-AUC of approximately 0.999, while maintaining a detection rate close to 98–99% at a false positive rate of 1% (Anderson & Roth, 2018). The strong performance of boosting methods on tabular security features is consistent with earlier work by Saxe and Berlin (2015), who demonstrated that ensemble models such as boosted decision trees often outperform deep neural networks when applied to structured malware metadata.

The success of boosting methods on EMBER led to widespread adoption of LightGBM as the standard baseline for static malware detection experiments. Subsequent studies comparing machine learning models for malware detection consistently reported that gradient-boosted decision trees remain highly competitive on structured feature representations (Anderson et al., 2018; Kolosnjaji et al., 2016). The effectiveness of boosting can be attributed largely to the nature of the EMBER feature space, which consists of structured numeric attributes extracted from PE files. Decision tree ensembles are particularly well suited to modeling such heterogeneous tabular features, allowing them to capture nonlinear relationships between attributes such as entropy statistics, section sizes, and imported API functions.

Another important methodological aspect emphasized in the EMBER paper is the use of time-aware train–test splits. Because malware evolves rapidly over time, Anderson and Roth recommended evaluating detection models using chronological splits that ensure training data precedes testing data temporally (Anderson & Roth, 2018). This evaluation protocol more closely resembles real-world deployment conditions in which models must detect malware samples that did not exist at training time. However, several later studies adopted random data splits, which may introduce temporal leakage when related malware samples appear in both the training and testing sets. Pendlebury et al. (2019) highlighted this issue in their systematic study of evaluation practices in malware machine learning, demonstrating that improper dataset splitting can significantly inflate reported performance metrics.

Taken together, these findings suggest that feature engineering plays a dominant role in static malware detection on EMBER, and that classical boosting algorithms remain a powerful baseline when operating on carefully constructed static features.

Several studies evaluating machine learning models on the EMBER dataset have observed that tree-based ensemble methods consistently outperform many alternative classifiers. Gradient-boosted decision trees, particularly LightGBM, achieve some of the highest detection performance due to their ability to effectively model structured PE feature representations (Anderson & Roth, 2018). Subsequent studies further confirmed that ensemble approaches such as Random Forest and boosted ensembles maintain strong detection capability across multiple evaluation scenarios, often outperforming neural network models when trained on the structured features provided by EMBER (Galen & Steele, 2020). These findings suggest that traditional ensemble learning techniques remain highly competitive for static malware detection tasks using engineered PE features.

References

Anderson & Roth (2018)

Galen & Steele (2020)

docs.title: Deep Neural Networks (2020–2022)
docs.text:
Following the widespread adoption of EMBER, several studies investigated whether neural architectures could outperform boosting models when trained on the dataset’s feature representation. One straightforward approach involved applying multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) to the feature vectors provided in the dataset. In these models, the 2,381-dimensional static feature vectors are fed directly into fully connected neural networks with nonlinear activation functions and dropout regularization. Empirical studies generally report ROC-AUC values between approximately 0.995 and 0.998 for such architectures, placing them close to—but rarely surpassing—the performance achieved by LightGBM models trained on the same data (Anderson & Roth, 2018).

The limited advantage of neural networks on EMBER-style data can be explained by the structure of the dataset itself. As noted in earlier work on malware classification, tree-based models tend to perform particularly well on tabular feature spaces with heterogeneous statistical distributions, whereas neural architectures provide greater benefits when operating on high-dimensional unstructured inputs such as images or sequential data (Saxe & Berlin, 2015).

Consequently, another line of research focused on end-to-end deep learning directly on raw executable bytes, removing the need for handcrafted feature extraction. One of the most influential architectures in this area is MalConv, proposed by Raff et al. (2017), which applies one-dimensional convolutional layers to raw byte sequences from executable files. MalConv demonstrated that convolutional neural networks can learn meaningful representations directly from raw binaries and achieve competitive malware detection performance without explicit feature engineering.

Subsequent studies expanded on this approach by improving convolutional architectures and introducing attention mechanisms for long binary sequences (Raff et al., 2018; Kolosnjaji et al., 2016). These models typically achieved detection accuracies ranging between 97% and 99%, depending on the dataset and evaluation protocol used. However, they often required significantly larger training datasets and greater computational resources compared with boosting models trained on structured static features. As a result, while deep neural networks demonstrated the feasibility of end-to-end malware classification, their performance advantages over classical machine learning models remained modest in the context of EMBER-style feature datasets.

docs.title: Graph-Based Approaches (2022–2024)
docs.text:
More recent research has explored incorporating structural information about program behavior into malware detection models using graph-based representations. In these approaches, relationships between components of a program: such as function calls, imported libraries, or control-flow dependencies are represented as graphs. These graph structures can then be processed using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which propagate information across nodes representing functions or API calls.

Graph-based malware detection techniques have been investigated in several studies. For example, Li et al. (2019) proposed a graph neural network framework that models relationships between API calls and program structures in order to capture semantic dependencies within malware binaries. Similarly, Feng et al. (2020) introduced GraphMal, which constructs graph representations from binary code and applies graph neural networks to classify malware samples. These approaches demonstrated that structural representations of software artifacts can capture information that may be difficult to represent using flat feature vectors.

Experimental evaluations of graph-based models on malware datasets have reported ROC-AUC values in the range of approximately 0.997–0.999, comparable to the performance of boosting models on EMBER-style feature datasets (Feng et al., 2020). Some studies have also suggested that graph-based representations may provide improved robustness at very low false positive rates, which are critical in practical antivirus deployment scenarios. However, evaluation methodologies vary widely across studies, and many experiments continue to rely on random train–test splits that may introduce temporal leakage. As noted by Pendlebury et al. (2019), such evaluation inconsistencies make it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the relative advantages of different modeling approaches.

docs.title: Transformer-Based Approaches (2022–2024)
docs.text:
Inspired by advances in natural language processing, researchers have recently begun exploring transformer architectures for malware detection. In these approaches, elements of executable programs—such as opcode sequences, byte streams, or API call traces—are treated as tokens in a sequence, allowing models based on self-attention to learn contextual relationships between program components.

Several studies have demonstrated the potential of transformer models for analyzing binary code. For example, Li et al. (2021) introduced a transformer-based framework for malware detection that models opcode sequences using self-attention mechanisms. Similarly, other work has applied transformer architectures to binary analysis tasks, showing that attention-based models can capture long-range dependencies in program structures that may be difficult for convolutional architectures to represent.

Experimental results reported in these studies suggest that transformer-based models can achieve detection performance comparable to or slightly better than traditional deep learning models, particularly in scenarios involving complex code semantics or obfuscation techniques. However, the computational cost of training transformer architectures on long binary sequences remains significantly higher than that of boosting models operating on static feature vectors. Consequently, while transformer-based methods represent a promising direction for malware analysis, their advantages on EMBER-style static feature datasets remain relatively modest.

docs.title: Adversarial Robustness Studies
docs.text:
Beyond detection accuracy, the EMBER dataset has also been widely used to investigate adversarial attacks against malware classifiers. In these studies, researchers explore how attackers can manipulate executable files in ways that preserve malicious functionality while causing machine learning models to misclassify the samples as benign.

Several works have demonstrated that static malware classifiers trained on EMBER-style features are vulnerable to feature-space adversarial attacks. Grosse et al. (2017) first explored the use of adversarial examples in malware detection models, demonstrating that gradient-based perturbations can cause neural classifiers to misclassify malicious binaries. Later work by Demetrio et al. (2019) introduced Malware Makeover, a framework that generates adversarial malware samples capable of evading static machine learning detectors. Similarly, Anderson et al. (2018) investigated practical evasion techniques against machine learning models used for malware detection, demonstrating that attackers can manipulate PE file features, such as imported functions or metadata fields, without affecting the functionality of the executable.

Empirical evaluations indicate that strong evasion attacks can significantly reduce detection performance. In some experiments, detection rates dropped from approximately 98% to below 60% when adversarial feature manipulations were applied (Demetrio et al., 2019). Defensive strategies such as adversarial training and feature hardening have been proposed to mitigate these vulnerabilities, although they often introduce trade-offs between robustness and classification accuracy.

docs.title: Temporal Trends on EMBER
docs.text:
Research on the EMBER 2018 has evolved through several methodological phases since its introduction by Hyrum S. Anderson and Phil Roth in 2018. During the initial period following the dataset’s release (approximately 2018–2020), studies consistently reported that gradient-boosted decision tree models, particularly LightGBM, achieved state-of-the-art performance when trained on the handcrafted static features provided by the dataset. The structured nature of the EMBER feature representation—comprising PE header metadata, entropy statistics, import tables, and section information—proved particularly well suited to boosting algorithms, which were able to capture nonlinear relationships between heterogeneous feature types. As a result, boosted tree ensembles quickly became the dominant baseline in the literature and were widely considered difficult to surpass when operating on tabular PE feature representations.

Between 2020 and 2022, researchers increasingly explored neural architectures in an attempt to determine whether deep learning models could outperform boosting approaches. Several studies evaluated multilayer perceptrons trained directly on EMBER feature vectors, while others investigated convolutional neural networks applied to raw executable bytes. Although byte-level models such as MalConv demonstrated the feasibility of end-to-end malware classification without handcrafted features, the improvements in detection performance relative to boosting methods were often limited. In many cases, neural models achieved performance comparable to—but not substantially better than—LightGBM classifiers, while requiring significantly greater computational resources for training and inference.

A further shift in research direction emerged between 2022 and 2024, as investigators began incorporating richer program representations into malware detection models. Rather than relying solely on flat feature vectors, these approaches introduced graph-based and sequence-based representations of executable programs. Graph neural networks were applied to structures such as import dependency graphs and function call graphs, while transformer architectures were used to analyze opcode sequences or byte streams as tokenized inputs. These methods aimed to capture deeper semantic relationships within binaries and to improve robustness against obfuscation. Despite these advances, empirical studies generally reported only marginal improvements over classical boosting baselines, particularly when evaluated on static feature datasets derived from EMBER.

More recent work has begun to explore foundation-style representation learning approaches, including self-supervised pretraining on large corpora of binaries and transfer learning across malware detection tasks. These approaches aim to learn general representations of binary code that can be adapted to multiple downstream tasks, potentially addressing limitations associated with handcrafted feature extraction. Nevertheless, the overall trend observed across the literature suggests that increasing model complexity has not translated into proportional improvements in detection performance on EMBER. Instead, the dataset has highlighted an important phenomenon in malware detection research: once strong static features are available, incremental improvements in model architecture often yield diminishing returns, indicating that future advances may depend more heavily on improved datasets, richer behavioral signals, and more realistic evaluation methodologies than on increasingly complex models alone.

docs.title: Dataset Bias
docs.text:
Despite its widespread adoption, the EMBER 2018 benchmark exhibits several forms of dataset bias that influence the performance of machine learning models trained on it. One important issue concerns the presence of packed versus unpacked malware samples. Packed malware often exhibits high entropy characteristics due to compression or encryption used to conceal malicious code. Because EMBER includes entropy-related features extracted from executable sections, machine learning models can implicitly learn simple heuristics that associate high entropy with malicious behavior. While such signals can improve detection performance within the dataset, they may also lead to overfitting to packing artifacts rather than actual malicious functionality, artificially inflating performance metrics. This phenomenon has been observed in several studies examining the role of entropy features in static malware detection.

Another form of bias arises from malware family imbalance within the dataset. Although EMBER contains a large number of samples, the distribution of malware families is not uniform. Certain families or campaigns may appear significantly more frequently than others, allowing models to effectively memorize patterns associated with those families rather than learning generalized indicators of malicious behavior. As a result, classifiers may achieve high detection rates on the dataset while performing poorly when encountering previously unseen families in real-world environments.

The benign portion of the dataset also introduces potential bias. A substantial fraction of benign samples correspond to standard Windows system binaries and commonly distributed software, which may exhibit structural characteristics that differ from benign software encountered in more diverse operational environments. This imbalance can create an unrealistic distinction between benign and malicious classes, enabling models to rely on superficial features that separate system binaries from malware samples rather than learning more robust indicators of malicious activity.

docs.title: Temporal Leakage
docs.text:
A critical methodological challenge in malware detection research involves temporal leakage, which occurs when training and test datasets contain samples that are temporally or structurally related. Because malware evolves continuously over time, effective evaluation requires ensuring that models are tested only on samples that appeared after the training data. The authors of the EMBER dataset therefore recommended the use of time-aware evaluation splits that respect the chronological order of sample collection.

In practice, however, many studies have relied on random train–test splits, which can inadvertently introduce related malware variants into both training and testing sets. Since malware families often generate numerous variants through automated packing or polymorphic techniques, random splitting can cause closely related samples to appear in both partitions. This leads to inflated evaluation results because models effectively learn to recognize variants of malware they have already seen during training. Studies analyzing evaluation practices in malware machine learning have shown that when proper chronological splits are enforced, detection performance can decrease by several percentage points in ROC-AUC—often by 2–5%—highlighting the extent to which temporal leakage can affect reported results. Consequently, the use of proper time-based evaluation has become an important methodological consideration when using EMBER.

docs.title: Label Quality
docs.text:
Another limitation of the dataset stems from the process used to assign malware labels. The ground-truth labels in EMBER are derived primarily from antivirus detections aggregated through VirusTotal, where a file is labeled malicious if it is flagged by a specified number of antivirus engines and benign if it receives no detections. While this approach enables large-scale dataset construction, it introduces several sources of uncertainty.

First, the threshold used to determine whether a sample is malicious is inherently arbitrary, as different studies may choose thresholds such as five or ten antivirus detections to classify a file as malware. Second, antivirus engines frequently disagree in their detections, particularly for newly emerging threats or ambiguous samples. Third, many antivirus engines share detection signatures and threat intelligence feeds, meaning that their predictions are not statistically independent. As a result, the aggregated label may not represent a reliable consensus. For these reasons, the labeling approach used in EMBER is often considered a form of weak supervision, where labels are derived from imperfect automated sources rather than manually verified ground truth.

docs.title: Generalization Across Datasets
docs.text:
An additional concern relates to the ability of models trained on EMBER to generalize to other malware datasets. Several cross-dataset experiments have demonstrated that classifiers trained on EMBER often experience noticeable performance degradation when evaluated on other large malware corpora such as SOREL-20M. This drop in performance suggests the presence of dataset-specific artifacts, where models learn patterns that are unique to the distribution of features present in EMBER rather than generalizable indicators of malicious behavior.

Similarly, models trained on SOREL-20M and evaluated on EMBER exhibit comparable performance degradation, further indicating that different malware datasets capture distinct distributions of executable characteristics. These results highlight an important limitation of many malware detection benchmarks: high performance on a single dataset does not necessarily translate into effective real-world deployment. Instead, robust evaluation requires cross-dataset validation and temporal testing to ensure that models generalize across different malware ecosystems.

docs.title: Reproducibility Issues
docs.text:
Reproducibility represents another challenge when working with EMBER. Although the dataset provides precomputed feature vectors, different studies often employ slightly different preprocessing pipelines when training their models. For example, some works normalize features before training, while others use raw feature values or apply custom feature transformations. In addition, researchers may adopt different VirusTotal detection thresholds when constructing subsets of the dataset, resulting in inconsistencies in label definitions across studies.

Another reproducibility limitation arises from the fact that EMBER does not provide raw executable binaries, but only extracted feature vectors and file hashes. Without access to the original binaries, it is difficult for researchers to verify feature extraction procedures or reproduce the dataset generation pipeline exactly. Over time, multiple unofficial preprocessing variants of the dataset have emerged, further complicating comparisons between studies that claim to use EMBER but rely on slightly different versions of the data.

docs.title: High-Level Thematic Synthesis
docs.text:
Despite these limitations, EMBER has had a profound impact on the development of machine learning approaches for malware detection. First, the dataset established gradient-boosted decision trees as a strong and reliable baseline for static malware detection tasks. Second, it demonstrated that increasing model complexity does not necessarily translate into improved performance when operating on structured static features, revealing diminishing returns for deep neural architectures in this context. Third, the dataset highlighted the importance of temporal evaluation protocols, encouraging researchers to consider the chronological evolution of malware when designing experimental methodologies.

Taken together, these insights underscore an important lesson for the field. The EMBER benchmark demonstrated that advances in model architecture alone are insufficient to guarantee improvements in malware detection performance. Instead, the structure of the dataset and the rigor of the evaluation methodology play a dominant role in shaping reported results.

docs.title: Limitations of EMBER and Motivation for New Datasets
docs.text:
Although EMBER remains one of the most widely used benchmarks for static malware detection research, it exhibits several limitations that restrict its applicability to real-world scenarios. The dataset does not fully reflect the class imbalance encountered in operational environments, where benign software vastly outnumbers malicious samples. Additionally, because the dataset contains only static feature representations, it cannot capture dynamic behavioral characteristics that may be necessary to detect sophisticated malware employing packing, polymorphism, or runtime obfuscation techniques. The reliance on VirusTotal detections also introduces uncertainty in label quality, while the static nature of the dataset limits the ability to model concept drift, where malware characteristics evolve over time.

These limitations have motivated the development of newer datasets designed to address some of these shortcomings. For example, the large-scale dataset SOREL-20M was introduced to enable research on massive-scale malware classification and weakly supervised learning, while EMBER 2024 extends the original benchmark with updated samples, improved labeling strategies, and additional tasks such as malware family classification. Together, these newer datasets represent an effort by the research community to build more realistic and comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating machine learning models in malware detection.

docs.title: BODMAS
docs.text:
The BODMAS dataset was introduced by Yang et al. as a large, timestamped collection of Windows PE binaries for malware analysis. It contains 57,293 malicious and 77,142 benign samples collected from Aug 2019 to Sept 2020, with carefully labeled family information (581 malware families) and 14 categories. It was introduced with an aim to embrace more recent malware belonging to multiple malware families.

Same format as EMBER and SOREL-20M

The dataset includes raw feature vectors instead of raw binaries, similar to EMBER dataset.

Feature Details Scale 134,435 total samples (57,293 malware and 77,142 benign). Data Types Pre-extracted EMBER v2 features (2,381 dimensions) and original PE binaries. Labels Binary labels (0/1) and family-level labels for multi-class tasks were retrieved from Blue Hexagon’s internal database, along with VirusTotal. Malware Families Categorized into 581 distinct families (e.g., WannaCry, Emotet, TrickBot). Temporal Scope Samples collected over a full year (August 2019 to August 2020), specifically to study model aging.

docs.title: Feature Extraction Method
docs.text: BODMAS uses the same format as EMBER and SOREL-20M. The dataset uses LIEF (Library to Instrument Executable Formats) to extract raw, static features directly from the Windows Portable Executable (PE) binaries. This process generates a fixed-size, 2,381-dimensional feature vector for every single file in the dataset.

docs.title: Label Source
docs.text: The researchers from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign partnered directly with the cybersecurity company Blue Hexagon to source both the files and the ground-truth labels. The malware was randomly sampled month-by-month from Blue Hexagon’s proprietary, internal malware database. The labels were carefully curated by professional security analysts.

docs.title: Curated Malware Family Labels
docs.text: BODMAS includes 581 curated malware labels, unlike EMBER and SOREL-20M, where reliable family-level ground truth is not provided. This enables multi-class classification research and family-wise drift analysis.

docs.title: More Recent Malware
docs.text:
• EMBER: mostly ≤ 2018
  • SOREL-20M: 2017–2019
  • BODMAS: 2019–2020

BODMAS was newer at release and contains post-2019 malware families.

docs.title: Realistic Benign-Malware Distribution
docs.text: BODMAS has 57k malware and 77k benign, so it is not perfectly 1:1 balanced. This is closer to real-world environments compared to datasets like EMBER, SOREL-20M, etc. thus reducing experimental bias.

docs.title: Research Works Using BODMAS
docs.text:
BODMAS: An Open Dataset for Learning‑based Temporal Analysis of PE Malware

Authors:

Limin Yang, Arridhana Ciptadi, Ihar Laziuk, Ali Ahmadzadeh, Gang Wang

Venue:

IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW), 2021

  • Introduces the BODMAS dataset for malware detection research

Dataset size:

  • 57,293 malware samples
  • 77,142 benign samples
  • 581 malware families.
  • Provides PE feature vectors similar to EMBER (2381 features).
  • Evaluates machine learning malware classifiers and discusses temporal concept drift.

In the 2024 study conducted by Buriro et al., researchers evaluated an anomaly detection approach for malware detection using the Blue Hexagon Open Dataset for Malware Analysis (BODMAS), which contains over 134,000 samples of malicious and benign Windows Portable Executable (PE) files. The study compared three machine learning classifiers—Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM)—by extracting features from the headers and sections of the PE files.

Distinct from traditional binary or multi-class methods that require both benign and malicious data for training, this research presents a one-class classification approach. This method is trained exclusively on benign samples to learn the profile of “normal” software, allowing it to detect unknown or zero-day malware as anomalies without any prior knowledge of malicious patterns. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest emerged as the most effective, achieving a peak accuracy of 99.73% while maintaining a zero False Positive Rate (or False Acceptance Rate) of malware.

Furthermore, the study contextualizes these results against multi-class classification tasks, such as those found in the MALW D&C framework, which not only distinguishes between malicious and benign files but also categorizes malware into specific families. While multi-class methods reported a high categorization accuracy of 97.69% using RF on set of selected features, the one-class anomaly detection approach demonstrated superior robustness in identifying deviations from normal behavior to prevent malware installation.

Classification Type Methodology Goal Reported Accuracy (RF) One-Class Trained only on benign samples. Detect unknown/zero-day malware as anomalies. 99.73% Binary Trained on both benign and malicious samples. Distinguish between malicious and benign files. 99.56% Multi-Class Trained on labeled malware families. Assign malware to different categories (e.g., Trojans, Spyware). 97.69%

H. Mohammadian et al. , developed a GNN-based malware detector that prunes large graphs for efficiency. Starting from BODMAS CFGs/FCGs, they apply graph reduction (e.g. leaf pruning) before running a GNN and GNNExplainer. Experiments on BODMAS show that Leaf Prune reduction actually improves performance: accuracy rises from ~94.5% (no pruning) to 95.4% (leaf pruning), with F1 ≈ 97.1%

Someya et al. utilized a curated subset of the BODMAS dataset, termed BODMAS-8cat (excluded packed/obfuscated samples and filtered out categories), to perform malware category classification rather than simple family attribution. Using an 8:2 hold-out validation, the model achieved a strong baseline accuracy of 95.04% on the test data. To further demonstrate the model’s ability to isolate critical malicious features, the authors evaluated classification accuracy using subgraphs consisting solely of the functions that received the highest attention weights. Remarkably, a subgraph containing just the top 1% of nodes—averaging only about six functions per sample—still yielded an accuracy of 69.67%. Expanding this to a 10% subgraph increased the accuracy to 71.73%, effectively proving that FCGAT can accurately characterize malware behavior relying on a surprisingly small fraction of the overall program.

Gokale et al utilizes three primary deep learning architectures—Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)—to detect malware in Windows Portable Executable (PE) files through the analysis of operation code (opcode) sequences and frequencies. Specifically applied to the BODMAS dataset, the study employed these models to capture the temporal dependencies inherent in sequential malware data, such as timestamps and SHA keys. Evaluation of these models on the BODMAS dataset yielded Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC-AUC) scores of 0.47 for the LSTM model, 0.46 for the GRU model, and 0.44 for the 1D CNN model. These results indicate that for the BODMAS samples, the recurrent models (LSTM and GRU) marginally outperformed the 1D CNN, though the researchers noted that further analysis is necessary to determine the most effective architecture for the dataset.

Model Architecture ROC-AUC (BODMAS) LSTM 0.47 GRU 0.46 1D CNN 0.44

Kim et al. proposes a deep learning framework designed to classify malware families using raw binary files, specifically to bypass the limitations of disassemblers that can be easily deceived by sophisticated packing and obfuscation.

The study introduces a multi-step approaches by considering two distinct types of static features -

  1. Malware Image - The binary file is converted into a grayscale image (byte-level granularity), which effectively represents global patterns but is sensitive to code obfuscation noise.
  2. Structural Entropy with Section Information - This modality uses Shannon entropy calculated from file chunks (chunk-level granularity). To enhance this feature, the researchers append one-hot encoded “section information” (e.g.,.text,.data, or “undefined”) extracted from the PE header. The highlight of this architecture is cross-model attention mechanism. This allows the model to learn byte-level and chunk-level information simultaneously, using one modality to compensate for the information loss. The researchers evaluated their model using a subset called BODMAS-14, which consists of 34,368 binaries from 14 malware families that contain more than 1,000 samples each.
Model Architecture Used Modality Accuracy F1-Score Baseline 7 (B7) Structural Entropy (w/ section info) 87.40% 0.8963 Baseline 8 (B8) Malware Image 87.94% 0.8831 Baseline 9 (B9) Entropy + Image (Simple Fusion) 92.57% 0.9380 Proposed Model Entropy + Image (Cross-Modal Attention) 92.92% 0.9415

Lu et al. introduces transformer-based approach to detect and classify malware using raw binaries. Two models have be used for the purpose - - SeqConvAttn - A sequence-based model that utilizes 1D convolution to compress raw byte sequences followed by transformer blocks to capture global dependencies within the file. - ImgConvAttn - An image-based model that applies a Vision Transformer (ViT) to classify malware based on greyscale or bigram frequency images. The research paper utilises a File-Aware-Two-Stage Framework, using faster ImgConvAttn model as the first stage. If the file is large (over 5 MB) or the first stage’s classification uncertainty exceeds a specific threshold, the file is rerouted to the more complex SeqConvAttn model. The researchers evaluated their models on two subsets of the BODMAS dataset: BODMAS-11 (the 11 largest malware families) and BODMAS-49 (families with at least 100 instances). The achieved scores are as follows:

Model / Framework BODMAS-11 Accuracy BODMAS-11 Weighted F1 BODMAS-49 Accuracy BODMAS-49 Weighted F1 SeqConvAttn 96.89% 96.90% 93.33% 92.90% ImgConvAttn (Frequency) 95.92% 95.90% 92.73% 92.30% TwoStage-fsa-25% 96.96% 96.96% 93.42% 92.98%

The use of self-attention allows the models to generate attention maps which highlight the specific sections of a binary file that the model deemed most appropriate for its classification decision. The framework achieves an average inference latency of 18.5 ms per file on the BODMAS-11 dataset when evaluated on a CPU. This is considered real-time performance compared to standard Tier 1 deep models

Compared to EMBER and SOREL-20M, BODMAS offers several unique advantages for PE-based malware detection research. It provides expert-curated malware family labels, enabling fine-grained classification and family-level drift analysis, which are not supported by EMBER or SOREL-20M. The dataset was explicitly structured for chronological evaluation, making it particularly suitable for concept drift and model adaptation studies. Additionally, BODMAS includes relatively recent malware samples (2019–2020) and adopts the standardized EMBER feature representation for reproducibility. Access to original malware binaries further enhances its applicability for structural and raw-byte research. These characteristics make BODMAS especially valuable for temporal robustness and semi-supervised malware detection research.

At the same time, there are few weaknesses we have to address - BODMAS’s total size (~0.13 M) is tiny relative to EMBER and especially SOREL-20M (≈20 M). Small-scale datasets tend to saturate performance (e.g. >99% AUC on EMBER) and have high variance at low false-positive rates. In practice, the modest size of BODMAS constrains large-scale or deep learning experiments (e.g. transformers or CNNs) and may yield over-optimistic results due to limited data coverage.

BODMAS covers only a ~13-month period (Aug 2019–Sep 2020). This narrow timeframe limits any long-term concept-drift analysis. Unlike datasets built from multiple years (SOREL spans 2017–2019), BODMAS alone cannot show malware evolution beyond 2020. Researchers must merge BODMAS with older data

Opcode-based sequential model (Gokhale et al) provide a baseline, but they face severe challenges on complex datasets like BODMAS compared to meta-feature approaches and fusion-based approaches (Kim et al.). The integration of structural entropy has been proven critical for maintaining performance on datasets that contain packed / obfuscated samples. Frameworks like TwoStage-fsa (Lu et al.) and leaf pruning GNNs (Mohammadian et al.) demonstrate that optimized model routing and graph reduction can enhance accuracy while drastically reducing inference latency, making them a good choice for real-time malware detection.

docs.title: SOREL-20M
docs.text:
SOREL-20M is a large-scale dataset containing nearly 20 million ﬁles (19,389,877) with pre-extracted features and metadata, along with nearly 10 million (9,919,251) binary samples of disarmed malware samples. It was released in late 2020 as a collaborati on between Sophos AI and ReversingLabs to provide the research community with a dataset that reflects the scale and complexity of real-world (production) malware detection environments.

SOREL-20M was specifically created to address the limitations of EMBER2018 (which has only ~1.1 million samples with single binary label based on a simple threshold rule)

Feature Details Scale 20 Million total samples (roughly 10M benign and 10M malicious). Data Types Includes pre-extracted EMBER v2 features, PE metadata, and disarmed binaries. Labels High-quality labels based on Sophos' internal detection systems. Multi-Target Unlike basic binary labels (0/1), it includes behavioral tags (e.g., ransomware, packer, spyware) and detection counts from different vendors. Time-Split Data is organized by "first-seen" time, allowing researchers to test for Concept Drift (how models perform on newer malware they haven't seen before). ### Large Dataset SOREL is nearly 20x larger than EMBER and 150x larger than BODMAS , which reduces variance when testing at very low False Positive Rates (FPR). Relatively smaller sizes of datasets cause the performance of classifiers to be saturated. ### Raw Binaries Unlike EMBER, which provides only static feature extractions, SOREL-20M includes 10 million raw binaries. This allows researchers to move beyond fixed metadata and explore the entire feature lifecycle—from custom extraction to deep learning on raw byte sequences. This also enables SOREL-20M to be a premier dataset for Adversarial Machine Learning. ### Labels In contrast to EMBER’s rigid binary labeling, SOREL-20M provides a rich metadata layer consisting of behavioral tags and cross-vendor detection counts. This multi-label architecture transforms the classification task from a simple binary decision into a complex multi-classification problem, enabling models to identify specific malware characteristics. Cross-vendor detection counts enable researchers to train the classifier to differentiate between a “high-certainty” malware (flagged by 40+ vendors) from a suspicious samples (flagged by only 2). ### Concept-Drift Analysis SOREL-20M includes “first-seen” timestamps in all the samples. This allows researches to experiment on Temporal Integrity and Concept-Drift Analysis.

docs.title: High Computational and Storage Barriers
docs.text: While the sheer-scale of SOREL-20M is it’s greatest strength, it also acts as a barrier when it comes to computation and storage. The full size of the dataset is 8TB and the complete contents of processed-data require approximately 552 GB of disk space. Due to the size of the dataset, training a boosted model is difficult. Training baseline models like LightGBM on the full dataset requires roughly 175 GB of RAM. Without a proper infrastructure, it is difficult to load and iterate through the dataset.

docs.title: Lack of Family Tags
docs.text: Despite the fact that SOREL-20M provides behavioural tags for all the samples, it lacks family-level labels that BODMAS provides. This makes it difficult to conduct family-level research.

docs.title: Outdated Samples
docs.text: SOREL-20M contains samples from 2017-2019. Several new techniques have been adopted by malware researchers to evade classifiers even after proper static feature analysis.

docs.title: Redundancy
docs.text: Recent studies have highlighted that large-scale malware datasets such as SOREL-20M contain significant duplication and family-level imbalance, which can artificially inflate model performance and lead to overly optimistic evaluation metrics.

docs.title: Research Works on SOREL-20M
docs.text:
Within the SOREL-20M literature, the Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) model, implemented via the LightGBM framework, stands as the most prominent traditional baseline. In the original SOREL-20M benchmark study, the LightGBM model was trained with 500 iterations and a maximum of 64 leaves per tree, utilizing a bagging fraction of 0.9

Richard et al. introduced SOREL-20M dataset and established baseline models on SOREL-20M using LightGBM and a PyTorch based Feed-Forward Neural Network.

Information derived from ROC curve with different baseline models are specified below -

Classifier Area Under the curve Feed-Forward Neural Network 0.998+-0.0000 LightGBM 0.981+-0.002

Almost all categories have an Area under the curve score above 0.97 with ransomware_tag performing the best (0.996) and adware_tag along with dowloader_tag performing the least (0.971 and 0.972 respectively), when tested using Feed-Forward Neural Network.

Malware Tag AUC Performance at Low FPR (10−4) Ransomware 0.996 Excellent (~85% TPR) File Injector 0.994 Good (~65% TPR) Worm 0.992 Moderate (~30% TPR) Spyware 0.984 Poor (<10% TPR) Traditional instance-based methods like k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) face extreme computational bottlenecks when applied to a 20-million-sample corpus. The storage of the raw 2381-dimensional features alone requires approximately 172 GB, and a standard kNN search would involve calculating the distance between a query point and every training point, which is computationally intensive.

While low-dimensional embeddings reduce feature dimensionality, the primary limitation of support vector machines (SVMs) in this context arises from the large number of training samples in SOREL-20M. Since SVM training complexity scales poorly with the number of samples, it remains computationally infeasible even with compact representations.

In a research by Rudd et al. Malware family classification on SOREL-20M is performed using a k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) classifier, where predictions are based on similarity to labeled training samples. The results show that performance depends on how similarity between malware samples is defined, with accuracies ranging from approximately 0.64–0.65 for simpler approaches to around 0.71–0.72 for more effective methods.

The authors demonstrate that learned low-dimensional representations significantly reduce storage requirements while preserving task performance. Specifically, the SOREL-20M dataset, which requires approximately 172 GB in its original feature form, can be compressed to around 2.3 GB using learned embeddings. This reduction enables efficient storage and faster computation, making large-scale malware analysis feasible even on resource-constrained systems.

Diaz and Bandala proposed a method that combines both LSTM and LightGBM, which yielded an accuracy of 91.73%. The ability to extract sequential patterns from data provides a better approach at detecting zero-day attacks.

docs.title: Self-supervised
docs.text: Miskell et al. introduces a self-supervised method, build upon raw PE byte sequences, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score of 78.6% with only 10% of the labelled data, thereby outperforming a traditional supervised CNN. In addition, the proposed method only requires 1 KB of header data, as opposed to baseline models, where 1 MB of header data is required

docs.title: CNN
docs.text: Wang et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of deep learning on raw opcode sequences. Their TextCNN-based approach achieved an accuracy of 91.93% on SOREL-20M, significantly outperforming traditional byte-level n-gram models and proving that instruction-level features provide a more robust representation of malicious intent. The researchers focused on key sections, especially the ones containing CALL instruction and significantly reduced the number of opcodes by 30.49% on SOREL-20M.

docs.title: AutoML
docs.text:
Brown et al. explores the application of Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) techniques for large-scale malware detection, with a focus on evaluating performance over the SOREL-20M benchmark. The study aims to eliminate the need for manual model design by leveraging Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to automatically construct optimal deep learning architectures, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Feedforward Neural Networks (FFNNs).

On the SOREL-20M dataset, the AutoML-derived models achieve high performance, reporting approximately 99.0% accuracy and an AUC of 0.998, outperforming or matching strong baselines such as LightGBM and manually designed neural networks. The results indicate that AutoML can effectively identify high-performing architectures without expert intervention, particularly in large-scale and noisy environments.

However, the study also highlights key limitations, including the significant computational cost associated with architecture search and the sensitivity to dataset characteristics such as redundancy and class imbalance

docs.title: Transformers
docs.text: Despite the success of transformer architectures in sequential domains, their application to large-scale tabular malware datasets such as SOREL-20M remains limited, highlighting a gap between modern deep learning approaches and practical large-scale malware detection benchmarks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Overall, existing research on SOREL-20M is heavily dominated by tabular machine learning approaches, with limited exploration of sequence-based or transformer-driven methods. This indicates a significant research gap in bridging structured feature representations with modern deep learning architectures, particularly in designing scalable models that can effectively leverage both semantic and structural characteristics of malware.

docs.title: Linux Based
docs.text: In contrast to PE-based malware research, which benefits from large-scale and standardized datasets such as SOREL-20M, ELF malware datasets remain fragmented and limited in scale, mainly due to diversity of Linux based systems - malware tailored to niche architecture, resulting in lack of comprehensive, large datasets compared to windows ecosystem.

docs.title: Antivirus Scanning
docs.text: Works on file signatures and heuristics.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text: Get the hash code of the malware and check with external sources.

docs.title: Host based signatures
docs.text: Host-based signatures, or indicators, are used to detect malicious code on victim computers. These indicators often identify files created or modified by the malware or specific changes that it makes to the registry. Unlike antivirus signatures, malware indicators focus on what the malware does to a system, not on the characteristics of the malware itself, which makes them more effective in detecting malware that changes form or that has been deleted from the hard disk

docs.title: Network signatures
docs.text: Network signatures are used to detect malicious code by monitoring net- work traffic. Network signatures can be created without malware analysis, but signatures created with the help of malware analysis are usually far more effective, offering a higher detection rate and fewer false positives.

docs.title: Basic Static Analysis
docs.text: Basic static analysis consists of examining the executable file without viewing the actual instructions. Basic static analysis can confirm whether a file is mali- cious, provide information about its functionality, and sometimes provide information that will allow you to produce simple network signatures. Basic static analysis is straightforward and can be quick, but it’s largely ineffective against sophisticated malware, and it can miss important behaviors.

docs.title: Basic Dynamic Analysis
docs.text: Basic dynamic analysis techniques involve running the malware and observ- ing its behavior on the system in order to remove the infection, produce effective signatures, or both. However, before you can run malware safely, you must set up an environment that will allow you to study the running malware without risk of damage to your system or network. Like basic static analysis techniques, basic dynamic analysis techniques can be used by most people without deep programming knowledge, but they won’t be effective with all malware and can miss important functionality.

docs.title: Advanced Static Analysis
docs.text: Advanced static analysis consists of reverse-engineering the malware’s internals by loading the executable into a disassembler and looking at the program instructions in order to discover what the program does. The instructions are executed by the CPU, so advanced static analysis tells you exactly what the pro- gram does. However, advanced static analysis has a steeper learning curve than basic static analysis and requires specialized knowledge of disassembly, code constructs, and Windows operating system concepts, all of which you’ll learn in this book.

docs.title: Advanced Dynamic Analysis

The instructions are executed by the CPU, so advanced static analysis tells you exactly what the pro- gram does. However, advanced static analysis has a steeper learning curve than basic static analysis and requires specialized knowledge of disassembly, code constructs, and Windows operating system concepts, all of which you’ll learn in this book.

docs.title: Types of Malware
docs.text: 1) Backdoor - Installs itself and exposes an access point in the host computer 2) Botnet - Infected hosts receive the same instructions from a single command-control server 3) Downloader - Downloads other malicious code. 4) Information-stealing malware - Collections information from a victim's computer and sends it to the attacker. 5) Launcher - Malicious program used to launch other malicious programs. (For stealth or greater access to a system) 6) Rootkit - Malicious code designed to conceal the existence of other code. Rootkits are usually paired with other malware. Makes the code difficult for the victim to detect. 7) Scareware - Malware designed to frighten an infected user. 8) Spam-sending malware - Sends spam, mainly for income. 9) Worm or virus - Malicious code that can copy itself and infect additional computers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The cyber-security landscape is constantly evolving. While major operating systems like Windows, Linux, and Android receive frequent updates to address critical vulnerabilities, malware creators continuously devise innovative methods to infect as many systems as possible. This challenge is compounded by the diverse nature of today’s digital ecosystem. From high-performance servers to embedded systems, the wide variety of hardware architectures makes it difficult to establish a unified approach to combat malicious software effectively.

At its core, malware refers to any piece of code specifically designed to compromise the (CIA) triad—Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability—of a system without the user's consent. While early forms of malware were limited to simple viruses that could be easily removed, the modern malware landscape has evolved into a complex array of threats, including ransomware, trojans, botnets, and rootkits. Modern malware payloads are characterised by their sophisticated evasion techniques. They employ advanced methods such as polymorphism and environmental awareness to remain undetected during inspections, only revealing their true nature under certain conditions. Additionally, recent malware often uses legitimate packers to disguise its harmful intent. This shift from static files to advanced and adaptive execution processes has created a detection gap that traditional methods struggle to address, leading to a need for intelligent, AI-based detection techniques.

Table of Recent Impactful Malware AttacksSource

Incident Year Primary Threat Main Consequence Change Healthcare 2024 BlackCat Ransomware National healthcare payment paralysis; $2B+ loss. **Heathrow and European Airport Disruption ** 2025 Ransomware Shutdown of airport operations across Europe, including major functions like check-in and boarding at Heathrow. Phishing Campaign against Ukrainain armed forces 2024 Infostealer Usage of malware tools to steal credentials from messaging platforms and internal systems, exposing secrets related to military operations. Snowflake Data Break 2025 Infostealer Exposed employee credentials, which were later used to break Snowflake’s cloud platform. Affected over 100 major organisations, including AT&T, Ticketmaster and Santander Bank.

docs.title: Traditional Malware Detection Methods
docs.text:
Various software applications use different algorithmic methods to identify malware in a system. The three primary methods for detecting malware are behavioural analysis, signature-based detection and heuristic analysis. A brief overview of each method is specified below.

  • Behavioural method - This method focuses on monitoring the behaviour of programs in real time in a controlled and safe environment. Instead of relying on known malware signatures, behavioural analysis observes how a file interacts with a system. If a program displays suspicious behaviour—such as attempting to access unauthorised files or established processes—it can be flagged and quarantined. This approach is particularly effective at identifying new or unknown malware variants that do not have established signatures.
  • Signature-based method - This is one of the commonly used techniques to detect malware, where a database containing signatures of known malware are stored and tested against software to establish whether it is a malware or not.
  • Heuristic-based method - Heuristic-based malware detection uses expert-defined rules, anomaly patterns and lightweight machine learning models. This method tries to generalise from previously observed malware behaviour and code characteristics.

docs.title: Why Traditional Sophisticated Signature-Based Method fails?
docs.text:
As the cybersecurity landscape undergoes continuous evolution, modern malware has increasingly adopted sophisticated techniques to circumvent traditional malware detection methodologies. Several illustrative examples are presented below: -

  • Polymorphic malware, exemplified by variants such as Emotet, Zeus, and TrickBot, demonstrates the capability to incessantly mutate its binary representation each time it is accessed or downloaded. This dynamic behaviour effectively enables these malicious entities to evade conventional signature-based malware detection mechanisms, posing significant challenges to defensive measures.
  • Contemporary malware exhibits a heightened awareness of its operating environment and employs advanced sandbox-evasion techniques to circumvent defensive measures. This includes the detection of virtualized environments and the implementation of execution delays, thereby masquerading as dormant.
  • Fileless malware that operates solely in memory and utilise legitimate system utilities poses a significant challenge to heuristic-based detectors, which predominantly rely on static malicious patterns and predefined rule sets.

These limitations highlight the weakness of modern, rule-based detection mechanisms against adaptive and sophisticated malware, motivating the shift towards data-driven, machine learning based malware detection system.

docs.title: AI Based Malware Detection Methodology
docs.text: In the recent years, focus on malware detection techniques has shifted from simple machine learning (Random Forest, SVM) to Deep Learning and Graph-Based approaches. Recent approaches model malware as structured program representations such as Control Flow Graphs (CFGs), rather than treating binaries as flat byte sequences. Ma et al. (2019) proposed a detection framework that leverages CFGs to extract deep semantic information from Android applications, achieving a high detection precision of 98.98% after the experiments were conducted on 10010 benign applications and 10683 malicious applications. Recent survey work by Grebehans et al (2025) identifies GAN as a primary tool for detecting and modelling adversarial threats in a dynamic environment. Unlike static analysis, dynamic GAN analyze API calls, system call traces and network connections. Retraining the defensive systems with synthetic adversarial threats renders detection stronger.
