docs.title: Dataset Taxonomy
docs.text:
To systematically understand the landscape of datasets used in research related to malware detection, we group them into three categories ****based on the tpye of analysis:

  1. Static Analysis Datasets – datasets derived without executing the malware (analyzing binaries, headers, permissions, sequences).
  2. Dynamic Analysis Datasets – datasets generated by executing malware in controlled environments to collect behavioral traces (API/system calls, sandbox logs, network activity).
  3. Hybrid Datasets – datasets that combine both static features and dynamic behavior for richer representations.

Each category plays a distinct role in machine learning-based malware detection, with trade-offs in feature complexity, computational cost, and resilience to evasive techniques.

docs.title: Static Analysis Datasets
docs.text:
Static analysis datasets remain widely used in both classical machine learning and modern deep learning research because they enable faster feature extraction without needing the execution of the binary. ****These datasets often include extracted features (PE header, byte sequences, disassembly opcodes, permissions) suitable for both traditional machine learning models and neural networks.

Key static malware datasets used in research:

  • EMBER 2018 – A large benchmark with feature vectors extracted from Windows PE files. It contains benign, malicious, and unknown samples and has been extensively used to evaluate ML classifiers.
  • EMBER2024 – A newer, larger version supporting multiple file formats and additional classification tasks those including malware detection, family classification, behavior identification.
  • SOREL‑20M – A very large PE corpus of around 20 million samples with feature vectors, widely used to push ML scalability.
  • BODMAS Dataset – A mid-scale PE dataset including raw binaries and extracted features with detailed malware family labels; often considered more balanced and recent than EMBER.
  • PE Malware Machine Learning Dataset – Public corpus with raw labeled PE binaries (~200 K+) that enables direct binary-level learning.
  • Other static benchmarks include Drebin-derived Android sets, MalImg image-based representations, and MalGenome for Android malware research.

Static features commonly used

  • PE headers, metadata (imports/exports).
  • Byte histograms and n-grams.
  • Opcode sequences or disassembly features.
  • Android APK permissions and intents.

Static datasets often support binary detection and family classification tasks and are amenable to both traditional ML (e.g., LightGBM, Random Forest) and deep models like CNNs on byte sequences.

docs.title: 2.2 Dynamic Analysis Datasets
docs.text:
Dynamic datasets arise from executing malware in isolated environments (e.g., Cuckoo/CAPE sandbox) and capturing behavioral artifacts such as API call traces, system calls, filesystem activity, and network traffic. These datasets better reflect runtime behavior and can detect evasive techniques that aren’t apparent when using static methods.

Prominent dynamic datasets include:

  • MalBehavD-V1 – A dataset of API call sequences obtained by executing Windows executables in sandbox environments.
  • Avast-CTU Public CAPE Dataset – Combines sandbox logs capturing rich behavioral traces suitable for ML tasks.
  • Cuckoo JSON Behavioral Reports – Community-shared dynamic logs (API calls, file activities) often used in behavior-centric ML research.
  • Dynamic Android Datasets (e.g., from CICMalDroid with dynamic logs) – These include runtime sequences and sometimes network traces.

Dynamic datasets tend to be smaller due to the cost of execution and collection but provide richer sequential features suitable for recurrent networks or temporal models.

docs.title: 2.3 Hybrid and Large-Scale Multimodal Datasets
docs.text:
Hybrid datasets combine static and dynamic aspects to capture a fuller representation of malware behavior, often required for robust detection.

  • Avast dynamic + static combined corpora – Some research has produced datasets that mix static feature extraction with behavior logs for family classification tasks.
  • MH-1M Android Malware Dataset – A recently released large collection with APK metadata and rich extracted attributes spanning many years, enabling studies on temporal drift and multi-feature learning.
  • Longitudinal Datasets (e.g., LAMDA) – Temporal Android benchmarks used to study concept drift, combining static features and longitudinal labeling across years.

docs.title: 2.4 Dataset Characteristics and Use-Cases
docs.text:
Dataset Year Approx. Size Type Label Source Typical Use Cases EMBER 2018 2018 ~1M feature vectors Static VT + internal labels Binary detection, ML benchmarks EMBER2024 2025 ~3.2M+ Static VT + challenge set Malware detection, family & behavior classification SOREL-20M 2020 ~20M Static Internal + telemetry Large-scale deep learning BODMAS 2020 ~134K Static VT + curated labels Balanced dataset, family studies MalBehavD-V1 2021 ~2.5K Dynamic VT + sandbox Behavioral sequence models Avast-CAPE 2022 ~50K+ Dynamic/Hybrid Sandbox traces Behavior analysis LAMDA 2025 ~1M+ Static/Temporal VT + temporal splits Concept drift studies MH-1M APKs 2025 ~1.3M Static-rich AndroZoo + VT Android multi-feature models

In conclusion, Static datasets (EMBER, SOREL-20M, BODMAS) are the most widely used in malware detection research due to scalable feature vectors and benchmarking tradition. Dynamic datasets (MalBehavD, CAPE) are less common but critical for behavior-oriented detection models. Hybrid/Longitudinal sets (LAMDA, MH-1M) reflect the field’s push toward multidimensional representations and temporal robustness. Dataset choice strongly influences model design. Static models favor gradient boosting and CNNs on embedded features, while dynamic/hybrid approaches lean on sequence learning and graph-based representations.

docs.title: EMBER
docs.text: EMBER was released by Endgame in 2018, EMBER (Endgame Malware Benchmark for Research) became the de-facto benchmark for static Windows PE malware detection using machine learning.

docs.title: Number of Samples
docs.text:
• ~1.1 million PE files total
    • ~900K labeled (train)
    • ~200K unlabeled (test/holdout style)
  • Roughly balanced benign vs malicious in labeled portion (~50/50, but not perfectly)

The dataset includes raw feature vectors instead of raw binaries and pre-extracted static features.

docs.title: Feature Extraction Method
docs.text:
EMBER uses handcrafted static PE features, extracted without execution:

Feature categories include PE header metadata (machine type, timestamp, section count), section information (names, entropy, sizes), imported/exported functions, data directories, byte histogram, byte-entropy histogram, string information, general file statistics with a total of dimensionality around 2,381 features.

docs.title: Label Source
docs.text:
Labels are derived from VirusTotal detections.

Typical labeling heuristic:

  • Malicious: detected by ≥ X AV engines (commonly 5+)
  • Benign: detected by 0 engines
  • Ambiguous: excluded or marked unlabeled

docs.title: Class Imbalance
docs.text: The official train split has approximately an equal amount of benign and malicious samples balanced, however, the family distribution is highly skewed. Moreover, packed malware is disproportionately represented and the real world imbalance that is required is not reflected. This ends up making EMBER more of a research based dataset than a realistic deployment dataset.

docs.title: Time Splits
docs.text: One of EMBER’s strengths is that it contains timestamp metadata. This is a consequence of the original paper that proposed chronological evaluation. however, many follow-up papers used random splits instead of temporal splits, causing leakage.

docs.title: Weaknesses
docs.text: Since the dataset doesn’t contain raw binaries, limitations are reached when trying deep byte-level modeling. There is also the added noise that comes from VirusTotal. It is limited by concept drift and can be used for statc analysis only. Handcrafted feature bias and Feature leakage risk coz of the timestamp feaature.

docs.title: Dominant Method: LightGBM
docs.text:
The official baseline used:

  • Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (LightGBM)
  • Achieved ROC-AUC ≈ 0.999
  • Detection rate ~98–99% at 1% FPR

Key assumptions:

  • Feature engineering sufficient
  • Static features generalize
  • Proper thresholding of VT labels

Temporal split usage:

  • Original work used time-aware split
  • Many later works reverted to random splits

docs.title: Thematic Insight
docs.text:
On EMBER, tree-based methods such as LightGBM consistently outperform deep neural networks when using handcrafted PE features, suggesting feature engineering still plays a dominant role in static malware detection.

This established a surprising result:

Deep learning did not immediately outperform boosted trees.

docs.title: Deep Neural Networks (2020–2022)
docs.text: Two main directions emerged:

docs.title: (A) MLPs on EMBER features
docs.text:
• Fully connected networks on 2,381 features
  • Performance similar or slightly worse than LightGBM
  • ROC-AUC typically 0.995–0.998

Finding:

  • Neural nets overfit easily
  • No significant gain over boosting

docs.title: (B) CNNs on Raw Bytes (not strictly EMBER)
docs.text:
Since EMBER lacks raw binaries, researchers:

  • Used other datasets for raw byte CNNs
  • Compared results conceptually against EMBER

Byte-level CNN models:

  • Achieved ~97–99% detection
  • Much heavier computational cost

Observation:

Raw byte learning did not drastically outperform structured features on EMBER-scale tasks.

docs.title: Graph-Based Approaches (2022–2024)
docs.text:
Some works constructed:

  • Import graphs
  • Function call graphs
  • Section dependency graphs

Applied:

  • Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)

Reported performance:

  • Comparable to LightGBM (ROC-AUC 0.997–0.999)
  • Slight improvements at low FPR regimes

Assumptions:

  • Graph structure encodes semantics
  • Static graph approximates behavior

Temporal splits:

  • Mixed usage
  • Many used random splits → potential leakage

docs.title: Transformer-Based Approaches (2022–2024)
docs.text:
Trend:

  • Treat opcode sequences or byte streams as language
  • Apply self-attention architectures

Performance:

  • Slight gains in low-FPR robustness
  • More robust to minor obfuscations

However:

  • Computationally expensive
  • Gains often marginal vs boosted trees on EMBER

docs.title: Adversarial Robustness Studies
docs.text:
EMBER became a testbed for:

  • Feature-space adversarial attacks
  • Evasion against tree models
  • Gradient-based attacks on MLPs

Findings:

  • LightGBM vulnerable to small feature perturbations
  • Static models can be evaded by:
    • Adding benign imports
    • Manipulating header metadata
  • Adversarial training improves robustness but reduces clean accuracy

Detection rate drop:

  • From ~98% to below 60% under strong evasion in some studies

Major assumption:

Attacker can modify PE features without breaking functionality.

docs.title: Family Imbalance
docs.text:
• Some families heavily represented
  • Detection becomes family memorization

docs.title: Benign Bias
docs.text:
• Windows system binaries dominate benign class
  • Unrealistic benign distribution

docs.title: Temporal Leakage
docs.text:
Major problem in literature:

Random splits:

  • Same malware family variants appear in train & test
  • Inflated performance

Proper time splits:

  • Performance drops 2–5% AUC
  • More realistic

Very few papers rigorously enforce chronological evaluation.

docs.title: Label Quality
docs.text:
VirusTotal-based labeling problems:

  1. Threshold selection arbitrary (5+ engines? 10+?)
  2. Disagreement among engines
  3. Engines share signatures → correlated errors

Thus:

Ground truth is weak supervision.

docs.title: Generalization
docs.text:
Cross-dataset studies show:

Train on EMBER → Test on SOREL:

  • Noticeable drop in performance
  • Distribution mismatch

Train on SOREL → Test on EMBER:

  • Similar drop

This suggests models partially learn dataset-specific artifacts.

docs.title: Reproducibility Issues
docs.text:
1. Feature extraction inconsistencies
  2. Different VT thresholds across papers
  3. Some use normalized features, others raw
  4. No raw binaries → cannot verify extraction

Also:

Multiple unofficial EMBER preprocessing variants exist.

docs.title: High-Level Thematic Synthesis
docs.text:
EMBER 2018 shaped the field in three ways:

  1. Established boosting as a strong baseline.
  2. Revealed diminishing returns of deep models on structured PE features.
  3. Exposed the importance of temporal evaluation.

Intellectually important insight:

EMBER demonstrated that model innovation alone does not guarantee performance gains; dataset structure and evaluation protocol dominate reported improvements.

This is analysis.

docs.title: Where EMBER 2018 Falls Short
docs.text:
• Not representative of real-world imbalance
  • Static-only (no behavioral resilience)
  • Susceptible to adversarial evasion
  • Limited modeling of concept drift
  • Weak label certainty

This directly motivated:

  • SOREL-20M for scale
  • EMBER 2024 for updated labeling and task diversity

docs.title: BODMAS
docs.text:
The BODMAS dataset was introduced by Yang et al. as a large, timestamped collection of Windows PE binaries for malware analysis. It contains 57,293 malicious and 77,142 benign samples collected from Aug 2019 to Sept 2020, with carefully labeled family information (581 malware families) and 14 categories. It was introduced with an aim to embrace more recent malware belonging to multiple malware families.

Same format as EMBER and SOREL-20M

The dataset includes raw feature vectors instead of raw binaries, similar to EMBER dataset.

docs.title: Feature Extraction Method
docs.text: BODMAS uses the same format as EMBER and SOREL-20M. The dataset uses LIEF (Library to Instrument Executable Formats) to extract raw, static features directly from the Windows Portable Executable (PE) binaries. This process generates a fixed-size, 2,381-dimensional feature vector for every single file in the dataset.

docs.title: Label Source
docs.text: The researchers from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign partnered directly with the cybersecurity company Blue Hexagon to source both the files and the ground-truth labels. The malware was randomly sampled month-by-month from Blue Hexagon's proprietary, internal malware database. The labels were carefully curated by professional security analysts.

docs.title: Curated Malware Family Labels
docs.text: BODMAS includes 581 curated malware labels, unlike EMBER and SOREL-20M, where reliable family-level ground truth is not provided. This enables multi-class classification research and family-wise drift analysis.

docs.title: More Recent Malware
docs.text:
• EMBER: mostly ≤ 2018
  • SOREL-20M: 2017–2019
  • BODMAS: 2019–2020

BODMAS was newer at release and contains post-2019 malware families.

docs.title: Realistic Benign-Malware Distribution
docs.text: BODMAS has 57k malware and 77k benign, so it is not perfectly 1:1 balanced. This is closer to real-world environments compared to datasets like EMBER, SOREL-20M, etc. thus reducing experimental bias.

docs.title: Research Works Using BODMAS
docs.text:
BODMAS: An Open Dataset for Learning‑based Temporal Analysis of PE Malware

Authors:

Limin Yang, Arridhana Ciptadi, Ihar Laziuk, Ali Ahmadzadeh, Gang Wang

Venue:

IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW), 2021

  • Introduces the BODMAS dataset for malware detection research

Dataset size:

  • 57,293 malware samples
  • 77,142 benign samples
  • 581 malware families.
  • Provides PE feature vectors similar to EMBER (2381 features).
  • Evaluates machine learning malware classifiers and discusses temporal concept drift.

In the 2024 study conducted by Buriro et al., researchers evaluated an anomaly detection approach for malware detection using the Blue Hexagon Open Dataset for Malware Analysis (BODMAS), which contains over 134,000 samples of malicious and benign Windows Portable Executable (PE) files. The study compared three machine learning classifiers—Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM)—by extracting features from the headers and sections of the PE files.

Distinct from traditional binary or multi-class methods that require both benign and malicious data for training, this research presents a one-class classification approach. This method is trained exclusively on benign samples to learn the profile of "normal" software, allowing it to detect unknown or zero-day malware as anomalies without any prior knowledge of malicious patterns. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest emerged as the most effective, achieving a peak accuracy of 99.73% while maintaining a zero False Positive Rate (or False Acceptance Rate) of malware.

Furthermore, the study contextualizes these results against multi-class classification tasks, such as those found in the MALW D&C framework, which not only distinguishes between malicious and benign files but also categorizes malware into specific families. While multi-class methods reported a high categorization accuracy of 97.69% using RF on set of selected features, the one-class anomaly detection approach demonstrated superior robustness in identifying deviations from normal behavior to prevent malware installation.

Classification Type Methodology Goal Reported Accuracy (RF) One-Class Trained only on benign samples. Detect unknown/zero-day malware as anomalies. 99.73% Binary Trained on both benign and malicious samples. Distinguish between malicious and benign files. 99.56% Multi-Class Trained on labeled malware families. Assign malware to different categories (e.g., Trojans, Spyware). 97.69% H. Mohammadian et al. , developed a GNN-based malware detector that prunes large graphs for efficiency. Starting from BODMAS CFGs/FCGs, they apply graph reduction (e.g. leaf pruning) before running a GNN and GNNExplainer. Experiments on BODMAS show that Leaf Prune reduction actually improves performance: accuracy rises from ~94.5% (no pruning) to 95.4% (leaf pruning), with F1 ≈ 97.1%

Someya et al. utilized a curated subset of the BODMAS dataset, termed BODMAS-8cat (excluded packed/obfuscated samples and filtered out categories), to perform malware category classification rather than simple family attribution. Using an 8:2 hold-out validation, the model achieved a strong baseline accuracy of 95.04% on the test data. To further demonstrate the model's ability to isolate critical malicious features, the authors evaluated classification accuracy using subgraphs consisting solely of the functions that received the highest attention weights. Remarkably, a subgraph containing just the top 1% of nodes—averaging only about six functions per sample—still yielded an accuracy of 69.67%. Expanding this to a 10% subgraph increased the accuracy to 71.73%, effectively proving that FCGAT can accurately characterize malware behavior relying on a surprisingly small fraction of the overall program.

Gokale et al utilizes three primary deep learning architectures—Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)—to detect malware in Windows Portable Executable (PE) files through the analysis of operation code (opcode) sequences and frequencies. Specifically applied to the BODMAS dataset, the study employed these models to capture the temporal dependencies inherent in sequential malware data, such as timestamps and SHA keys. Evaluation of these models on the BODMAS dataset yielded Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC-AUC) scores of 0.47 for the LSTM model, 0.46 for the GRU model, and 0.44 for the 1D CNN model. These results indicate that for the BODMAS samples, the recurrent models (LSTM and GRU) marginally outperformed the 1D CNN, though the researchers noted that further analysis is necessary to determine the most effective architecture for the dataset.

Model Architecture ROC-AUC (BODMAS) LSTM 0.47 GRU 0.46 1D CNN 0.44 Kim et al. proposes a deep learning framework designed to classify malware families using raw binary files, specifically to bypass the limitations of disassemblers that can be easily deceived by sophisticated packing and obfuscation.

The study introduces a multi-step approaches by considering two distinct types of static features -

1) Malware Image - The binary file is converted into a grayscale image (byte-level granularity), which effectively represents global patterns but is sensitive to code obfuscation noise. 2) Structural Entropy with Section Information - This modality uses Shannon entropy calculated from file chunks (chunk-level granularity). To enhance this feature, the researchers append one-hot encoded "section information" (e.g.,.text,.data, or "undefined") extracted from the PE header. The highlight of this architecture is cross-model attention mechanism. This allows the model to learn byte-level and chunk-level information simultaneously, using one modality to compensate for the information loss. The researchers evaluated their model using a subset called BODMAS-14, which consists of 34,368 binaries from 14 malware families that contain more than 1,000 samples each.

Model Architecture Used Modality Accuracy F1-Score Baseline 7 (B7) Structural Entropy (w/ section info) 87.40% 0.8963 Baseline 8 (B8) Malware Image 87.94% 0.8831 Baseline 9 (B9) Entropy + Image (Simple Fusion) 92.57% 0.9380 Proposed Model Entropy + Image (Cross-Modal Attention) 92.92% 0.9415

Lu et al. introduces transformer-based approach to detect and classify malware using raw binaries. Two models have be used for the purpose - - SeqConvAttn - A sequence-based model that utilizes 1D convolution to compress raw byte sequences followed by transformer blocks to capture global dependencies within the file. - ImgConvAttn - An image-based model that applies a Vision Transformer (ViT) to classify malware based on greyscale or bigram frequency images. The research paper utilises a File-Aware-Two-Stage Framework, using faster ImgConvAttn model as the first stage. If the file is large (over 5 MB) or the first stage's classification uncertainty exceeds a specific threshold, the file is rerouted to the more complex SeqConvAttn model. The researchers evaluated their models on two subsets of the BODMAS dataset: BODMAS-11 (the 11 largest malware families) and BODMAS-49 (families with at least 100 instances). The achieved scores are as follows:

Model / Framework BODMAS-11 Accuracy BODMAS-11 Weighted F1 BODMAS-49 Accuracy BODMAS-49 Weighted F1 SeqConvAttn 96.89% 96.90% 93.33% 92.90% ImgConvAttn (Frequency) 95.92% 95.90% 92.73% 92.30% TwoStage-fsa-25% 96.96% 96.96% 93.42% 92.98% The use of self-attention allows the models to generate attention maps which highlight the specific sections of a binary file that the model deemed most appropriate for its classification decision. The framework achieves an average inference latency of 18.5 ms per file on the BODMAS-11 dataset when evaluated on a CPU. This is considered real-time performance compared to standard Tier 1 deep models

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Study Methodology Primary Contribution Key Metric on BODMAS Buriro et al. One-Class Random Forest Anomaly detection trained only on benign samples to detect zero-day threats. 99.73% Accuracy (One-Class) Lu et al. Two-Stage Transformer (TwoStage-fsa) A file-size-aware framework using image and sequence transformers to balance latency and accuracy. 96.96% Accuracy (BODMAS-11) H. Mohammadian et al. Pruned GNN Pruning "leaf nodes" from Control Flow Graphs to improve graph processing efficiency. 95.4% Accuracy / 97.1% F1 Someya et al. FCGAT (Attention GNN) Category classification using function subgraphs; isolated critical malicious behavior in just 1% of code. 95.04% Baseline Accuracy Kim et al. Cross-Modal 1D-CNN Fuses malware images and structural entropy via attention to bypass packing/obfuscation. 92.92% Accuracy (BODMAS-14) Gokhale et al. Stacked RNN/CNN Analyzes opcode frequency and sequential dependencies using LSTM and GRU architectures. 0.47 ROC-AUC (LSTM)

Compared to EMBER and SOREL-20M, BODMAS offers several unique advantages for PE-based malware detection research. It provides expert-curated malware family labels, enabling fine-grained classification and family-level drift analysis, which are not supported by EMBER or SOREL-20M. The dataset was explicitly structured for chronological evaluation, making it particularly suitable for concept drift and model adaptation studies. Additionally, BODMAS includes relatively recent malware samples (2019–2020) and adopts the standardized EMBER feature representation for reproducibility. Access to original malware binaries further enhances its applicability for structural and raw-byte research. These characteristics make BODMAS especially valuable for temporal robustness and semi-supervised malware detection research.

At the same time, there are few weaknesses we have to address - BODMAS’s total size (~0.13 M) is tiny relative to EMBER and especially SOREL-20M (≈20 M). Small-scale datasets tend to saturate performance (e.g. >99% AUC on EMBER) and have high variance at low false-positive rates. In practice, the modest size of BODMAS constrains large-scale or deep learning experiments (e.g. transformers or CNNs) and may yield over-optimistic results due to limited data coverage.

BODMAS covers only a ~13-month period (Aug 2019–Sep 2020). This narrow timeframe limits any long-term concept-drift analysis. Unlike datasets built from multiple years (SOREL spans 2017–2019), BODMAS alone cannot show malware evolution beyond 2020. Researchers must merge BODMAS with older data

Opcode-based sequential model (Gokhale et al) provide a baseline, but they face severe challenges on complex datasets like BODMAS compared to meta-feature approaches and fusion-based approaches (Kim et al.). The integration of structural entropy has been proven critical for maintaining performance on datasets that contain packed / obfuscated samples. Frameworks like TwoStage-fsa (Lu et al.) and leaf pruning GNNs (Mohammadian et al.) demonstrate that optimized model routing and graph reduction can enhance accuracy while drastically reducing inference latency, making them a good choice for real-time malware detection.

docs.title: Feature Set Description
docs.text: The EMBER dataset distinguishes between raw features and model features. The dataset is organized into 8 groups, categorized as either parsed or format-agnistic A Portable Executable (PE) file is the standard file format for executables, object code, and shared libraries (DLLs) used in 32-bit and 64-bit versions of Windows operating systems.

docs.title: 1. The Standard Headers
docs.text:
Headers serve as the "map" for the Windows loader, providing a summary of what the file contains.

  • COFF File Header: This contains foundational data, including the target machine type, the nature of the file (EXE vs. DLL), and the count of sections and symbols.

  • Optional Header: Despite its name, it is essential for executables. It identifies the linker version, code size, data size, and the Entry Point (where the program starts).

  • Data Directories: Located within the Optional Header, these act as pointers to tables for imports, exports, resources, and certificates.

  • Section Table: This functions as a directory, outlining the name, memory offset, and size of every section in the file.

docs.title: Additional Headers
docs.text:
• Import Address Table (IAT)

The Import Address Table acts as a lookup table used by the windows loader to connect your program with functions stored in external libraries

  • When we run .exe, the windows loader looks at IAT, finds the necessary DLLS, and fills the table with the actual memory address of those functions.

  • Security researchers monitor the IAT because it reveals what a program is capable of doing. For example, if a small file imports InternetOpen and WriteProcessMemory, it is a high-risk indicator of malicious behavior.

docs.title: Thread Local Storage (.tls)
docs.text:
The .tls section is designed to store data that is unique to each thread in a multi-threaded application.

  • This is an array of memory addresses. Each address points to a function that the Windows loader must run immediately after mapping the file into memory but before the main thread.
Section Name Purpose .text Contains the executable machine code. .data / .rdata Stores initialized global and static variables (read/write or read-only). .bss Contains uninitialized data. .reloc Stores relocation tables used to reassign a base address if the preferred one is unavailable. .rsrc Holds resources for user interfaces, such as icons, bitmaps, and menus. Data Format Best Model Type Example Dataset Tabular / JSON Features GBDT (LightGBM/XGBoost) EMBER, BODMAS Binary Images CNN Malimg Raw Byte Sequences 1D CNN / MalConv Sorel-20M (Raw) Code Graphs GNN Devign, Big-Vul

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
• Methods to perform detection and anlysis of malware attcaks using AI
  • Find some method that has been worked on and has proved to be useful and which could be worked upon to create some novel thing
Component Role in your "Fight" Extension for Novelty The Attacker (Generator) Mutates malware to bypass the detector. Novelty: Use a Conditional GAN (cGAN) that generates malware for specific targets (e.g., IoT vs. Windows). The Defender (Discriminator) Learns to flag both real and synthetic malware. Novelty: Integrate XAI (SHAP/LIME) so the defender reports which "features" (e.g., specific API calls) were suspicious. The Referee (RL Agent) Rewards the Generator for evasion AND the Defender for detection. Novelty: The RL agent manages the "difficulty" of the fight, preventing the GAN from collapsing. How it prevents: An RL agent monitors the system. If it sees the first sign of a GAN-generated attack, it doesn't just "flag" it; it automatically cuts the network connection or quarantines the process in a sandbox instantly.

docs.title: Analysis of the BODMAS Malware Dataset in Recent Research
docs.text:
The BODMAS dataset was introduced by Yang et al. (IEEE SPW 2021) as a large, timestamped corpus of Windows PE binaries for malware analysis

. It contains 57,293 malicious and 77,142 benign samples collected from Aug 2019 to Sept 2020, with carefully labeled family information (581 malware families, 14 high-level categories). Its design explicitly targets temporal analysis: samples are timestamped so that concept drift (changes over time) can be studied. The authors emphasize these strengths (recency and rich labeling) as key contributions. According to Google Scholar, the original BODMAS paper has been widely cited (≥147 citations)

, reflecting its impact as a benchmark dataset.

Despite these strengths, later work has noted limitations. For example, Zhou et al. (NDSS 2025) critique BODMAS as outdated, observing that it “provides only malware binaries from five years ago”

(i.e. only through 2020). In practice, this motivates new, more up-to-date datasets. We summarize below how select top-tier works use or evaluate BODMAS, highlighting what each finds positive or problematic about the dataset.

docs.title: Key Papers Using or Analyzing BODMAS
docs.text:
• Yang et al. (IEEE SPW 2021)

– Original BODMAS dataset release (147 citations). The paper introduces BODMAS and describes its scope: ~57K malware, ~77K benign, timestamped (2019–2020), with well-curated family labels. Its contributions are explicitly the recency of samples and inclusion of detailed labels for both malware and benign files. (The benign binaries are provided via features due to licensing; the focus is on enabling learning-based malware analysis.) The authors perform preliminary concept-drift analyses using BODMAS, showing how classifier accuracy degrades over time. Overall, BODMAS’s strengths are its size, timestamps, and label richness, which have since made it a popular benchmark (noted by its high citation count- ). One limitation (noted indirectly by others) is its fixed time span – new variants beyond 2020 are not covered.

  • Chen et al. (USENIX Security 2023)

– Active Learning for Malware Detection. This study evaluates active learning strategies for PE malware classification. It cites the BODMAS paper as prior work: “BODMAS… compared the following active learning sample selection schemes: random, uncertain, and non-conformity score” and found that uncertainty sampling performed best. In other words, Chen et al. use BODMAS to validate sampling methods: they leverage the BODMAS dataset (labels from 2019–2020) to compare how different query strategies affect learning. This work thus confirms and extends BODMAS’s value in studying retraining: the authors note that BODMAS showed uncertainty-based sampling to be very effective- . They do not criticize BODMAS explicitly, but their use of it underlines its role as a modern PE malware benchmark.

  • Gibert et al. (CCS 2023, Workshop)

– Certified Robustness against Patch/Appends. This workshop paper adapts ideas from randomized smoothing to malware. Crucially, the authors train and test on BODMAS: they “trained a classifier with our chunk-based scheme on the BODMAS dataset” and demonstrate that their “chunk-based smoothed classifier is more robust against…evasion attacks” than a standard model- . In other words, BODMAS is used as the benchmark for evaluating a novel defense. The authors implicitly confirm BODMAS’s adequacy by using it for training. They do not critique the dataset, but their results show that even on BODMAS’s relatively recent samples, robustness against attacks is a key concern.

  • Zhou et al. (NDSS 2025)

– Concept-Drift Adaptation in Windows Malware. In this forthcoming NDSS paper, the authors build a new dataset spanning 2024 to study drift. They contrast their data with existing ones, noting: “The BODMAS dataset… provides only malware binaries from five years ago”

  • . This is a direct limitation: since BODMAS stops at 2020, it lacks current malware families. Zhou et al. highlight this gap as motivation for a new dataset. They also note that BODMAS (being Windows-focused) and another dataset (EMBER) are outdated, and thus their MB-24 dataset (2024 malware) offers a more realistic testbed. Thus, this work explicitly criticizes BODMAS’s recency, using it as an example of older research data that must be refreshed.

docs.title: Comparison of Selected Studies
docs.text:
The table below summarizes the above papers and others with BODMAS ties, noting how they use or assess the dataset and key takeaways:

Paper (Venue, Year) Citations BODMAS Usage Notes on Strengths/Limits Yang et al. (IEEE SPW 2021) 147 Introduced BODMAS (open PE malware dataset) – 57,293 malware + 77,142 benign, timestamped (2019–2020), with 581 families . Highlights recent timestamped samples and rich labeling (families/categories) as strengths . Enables concept-drift analysis. Chen et al. (USENIX Sec 2023) (–) Used BODMAS to compare active-learning strategies. Found that uncertainty sampling on BODMAS data performs very well . Confirms BODMAS’s utility as a modern benchmark for learning algorithms. No major critique noted. Gibert et al. (CCS 2023 Workshop) (–) Trained a chunk-based smoothed malware classifier on BODMAS. Showed improved robustness against patch/append attacks on BODMAS samples . Uses BODMAS to demonstrate defense effectiveness. Implies dataset is suitable for evaluating adversarial robustness. Zhou et al. (NDSS 2025) (–) Critiques existing datasets: notes BODMAS only covers “malware binaries from five years ago” . Uses BODMAS as a point of comparison when building a new 2024 dataset. Points out BODMAS’s outdated timeline (stopping in 2020) as a limitation, motivating newer data collection.

Each of these works appears in a top-tier venue (USENIX Security, CCS, NDSS). They either use BODMAS for evaluation (as a benchmark training/test set) or analyze it (e.g. assessing sample-selection methods or its recency). Overall, BODMAS’s strengths – recent, real-world samples with family labels – have made it a popular reference point, while its chief limitation is its finite time coverage.

Sources: Key details are drawn from the cited papers. Yang et al.’s original BODMAS paper describes the dataset’s contents and goals

. Chen et al. summarize prior BODMAS-based experiments, Gibert et al. explicitly report training on BODMAS, and Zhou et al. highlight BODMAS’s obsolescence

. These references anchor the above analysis.

I’ll get back to you shortly with a focused analysis based on that.

  1. Usage in Experiments: The authors include BODMAS as one of two Windows PE datasets

. BODMAS files (2,381 static features each) span October 2019–September 2020. They use October–December 2019 data for training, January–March 2020 for validation, and April–September 2020 for testing. Hyperparameters are tuned on BODMAS and then applied to the EMBER dataset. Beyond binary malware detection, BODMAS is also used for an 11-class malware-family task (top-10 families + benign). In that multiclass setting (with the same temporal splits), XGBoost on BODMAS achieves ~71% F1 (improving slightly to ~71.4% with ADAPT). The dataset is likewise used in an active-learning scenario (50 samples/month), where ADAPT+AL boosts BODMAS F1 by about 3% over a random sampling baseline- .

  • Pros/Strengths: According to the paper, BODMAS is a well-structured, real-world Windows malware corpus with consistent static features

. It yields very high baseline detection accuracy: for example, a vanilla XGBoost model already achieves ~99.2% F1 on BODMAS. This indicates that BODMAS’s classes are well-separated and its distribution is relatively stable over time. ADAPT (the proposed method) further marginally improves this, raising XGBoost’s F1 by ~0.4% while also reducing both false positives and false negatives. In other words, BODMAS’s stability allows tree-based models to perform extremely well, and ADAPT simply maintains or slightly enhances that high performance across the test period. In the active-learning experiment, ADAPT’s integration improves BODMAS results (e.g. +3% F1)- , again reflecting the dataset’s amenability to semi-supervised tuning.

  • Cons/Limitations: The paper notes that BODMAS exhibits very little concept drift (“less pronounced effect”)

. While this makes BODMAS easy for the models (hence the ~99% F1), it also limits the dataset’s challenge for drift-robust methods. In fact, none of the self-training baselines beats the plain XGBoost on BODMAS, so adaptation yields only a tiny gain (0.4% F1). Thus, BODMAS’s limited drift means there’s little room to demonstrate ADAPT’s benefit – a fact the authors highlight. In the multiclass setting, the task is tougher (baseline F1 ~71%), but even there ADAPT’s improvements are modest. In summary, the authors imply that BODMAS’s very high baseline accuracy (and imbalanced/malware-heavy composition) reflects a dataset with minimal drift; this makes it less revealing for evaluating concept-drift adaptation and constrains the observable gains from advanced methods

docs.title: Observed Properties of BODMAS
docs.text:
The BODMAS dataset is a large Windows PE malware collection (57,293 malicious vs. 77,142 benign samples

) covering August 2019–September 2020. Each sample is represented by a standard 2381-dimensional static feature vector (Ember format). It includes rich metadata: timestamps (chronologically sorted) and expert-curated family labels (581 malware families). These features yield very high separability – for example, classifiers on BODMAS typically achieve ≈97–99% F1 after periodic retraining. In practice, the paper notes only a modest degradation over time: concept drift exists but is mild (with retraining F1 remaining above ~96%

).

docs.title: Practical Strengths
docs.text:
• Large, Up-to-date Benchmark. BODMAS’s size and recency (data from 2019–2020) make it a rigorous testbed for modern malware detection

  • .

  • Consistent Feature Space. Using the Ember/LIEF feature format (2381 dims)

  • means models can leverage well-established static features consistently across all samples.

  • Rich Labels. Having timestamp and family labels enables temporal and family-based analyses; it supports both binary detection and multi-class attribution tasks.

  • Balanced Diversity. BODMAS contains many benign and malware samples, so it approximates a realistic benign:malware ratio and helps benchmark classifiers at scale.

  • High Baseline Performance. The strong class separability (e.g. ~97–99% F1 with retraining

  • ) means that even simple models perform very well, making BODMAS useful as a “solved” reference to compare new techniques.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Moderate Concept Drift. Because the dataset spans only one year with steadily accumulating new families, the implied drift is relatively low. The original analysis showed only slight performance drop on newer samples

  • . In ADAPT’s context, this suggests less room for improvement from drift-adaptation techniques on BODMAS.

  • Class Imbalance. BODMAS has more benign than malware samples (∼1.35:1 ratio

  • ). While not extreme, this mild imbalance can bias learning and is noted by the authors in related work.

  • Homogeneous Data Domain. All samples are Windows executables with static features; there are no dynamic or network behaviors. Thus BODMAS does not capture cross-platform or behavioral aspects of malware.

  • Labeling Restrictions. (As noted by the dataset providers) benign binaries are not freely shared, limiting some forms of analysis.

  • Time Span. The one-year window may omit longer-term trends. BODMAS focuses on recent malware, so it may miss older or future-scope drifts.

In summary, the ADAPT paper’s use of BODMAS suggests a dataset that is large, up-to-date, and “clean” (well-labeled with little noise), leading to very high baseline accuracy. These traits make BODMAS a valuable benchmark

, but also imply limited concept drift challenge and some benign skew, which one must account for in evaluation

.

Sources: Dataset summary and analysis from the BODMAS publication and documentation

(as reflected by the ADAPT paper’s experimental context).

docs.title: ByteEnc: Malware Detection Using Transformer Encoders
Summary
docs.text: The ByteEnc research introduces a specialized Transformer encoder-based language model designed to detect malware in non-executable files, such as PDFs, MS Office documents, and HWP (Hangul Word Processor) files, by analyzing their raw byte sequences111111111.

docs.title: Core Methodology
docs.text:
• Byte-Level Analysis: The model treats raw byte sequences within files like character sequences in a document, assuming that malicious actions follow underlying semantic patterns2222.

  • Transformer Architecture: ByteEnc uses stacked Transformer encoders (similar to BERT) to understand these sequences globally rather than focusing only on local patterns3333.

  • Unigram Tokenization: To avoid "out-of-vocabulary" issues caused by new operational keywords or software updates, the model uses byte-level unigram tokenization, where each individual byte is treated as a single token444444444.

  • Relative Positional Embedding (RePE): Instead of absolute positions, the model uses relative positional information. This is more effective for malware detection because malicious actions are often composed of small fractions scattered throughout a file5555.

docs.title: Pre-training Strategies
docs.text:
The researchers developed two novel pre-training algorithms specifically designed for the characteristics of byte sequences6:

  • Real-or-Fake Prediction (RFP): A token-level binary classification task where the model predicts if a byte is "real" (original) or "fake" (a randomly replaced corrupted byte)7777.

  • Same-Sequence Prediction (SSP): A sequence-level task where the model predicts if two sub-sequences originated from the same original file. This encourages the model to understand patterns at a file-wide level888888888.

  • Combined Approach: The researchers found that combining Masked Language Modeling (MLM) with SSP provided the best overall performance9999.

docs.title: Key Findings and Performance
docs.text:
• Superior Accuracy: ByteEnc consistently demonstrated significantly better performance than traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), such as MalConv and SPAP, across all file formats10101010.

  • Performance Gains: The model achieved an improvement in Macro F1 scores of approximately 2.7% to 11.1% compared to previous CNN-based models11.

  • Cross-Format Knowledge: A significant finding was that a model pre-trained only on one format (e.g., HWP) still performed effectively when detecting malware in different formats like PDF and MS Office12121212.

  • Scalability: Larger versions of the model (BERT-base size with 110M parameters) generally outperformed smaller versions (BERT-small with 29M parameters), as they were better at capturing complex sequential patterns131313131313131313.

docs.title: Limitations and Future Work
docs.text:
• Sequence Length: The current model uses an input window of 512 bytes. This may be insufficient for formats like HWP, where malicious actions can be spread across very long byte sequences (up to 710K bytes)141414141414141414.

  • Dataset Imbalance: The researchers noted that the model's reliability (sensitivity) could be further improved by continuing to collect and annotate more balanced datasets to better represent malicious cases15151515.

docs.title: Malware Detection and Classification Using Generative Adversarial Network
docs.text: The newly uploaded report, "Malware Detection and Classification Using Generative Adversarial Network" (2024), focuses on using Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) to solve the common problem of imbalanced datasets and the detection of "unseen" or zero-day malware1111.

docs.title: Core Methodology: The CGAN Approach
docs.text:
Unlike basic GANs, the proposed CGAN model uses label information to guide both the generator and discriminator, making the learning process more structured2.

  • Adversarial Training: The work uses a "minimax two-player game" where a Generator creates synthetic malware samples from random noise, and a Discriminator learns to distinguish these "fake" samples from real malware3333.

  • Image-Based Representation: The system treats malware as images. It was tested on two specific types:

    • Grayscale Images: Using the Malimg dataset (9,339 samples across 25 classes) resized to $224 \times 224$ pixels4.

    • RGB Images: Using the IEEE DataPort dataset (24,109 samples) for binary classification (Malicious vs. Normal)5.

  • Robustness: By including these synthetic, GAN-generated adversarial samples in the training process, the final detection model becomes significantly more robust against sophisticated and novel malware variants.

docs.title: Model Architecture
docs.text:
• Generator: Utilizes a fully connected layer followed by several Convolution2D Transpose layers to "up-sample" a small input vector into a full-sized $224 \times 224$ fake image7.

  • Discriminator: Uses 2D Convolution layers and LeakyReLU layers, ending with a Sigmoid activation function to provide a final "Real or Fake" binary output8888.

docs.title: Performance and Key Results
docs.text:
The research compared two versions of the model: CGAN Model1 (using the Adam optimizer) and CGAN Model2 (using the SGD optimizer)9.

  • Accuracy:

    • Multiclass Classification (Malimg): CGAN Model1 achieved 96.96% accuracy, outperforming several state-of-the-art models like DCGAN (90%) and E-GAN (96.35%)10101010101010.

    • Binary Detection (IEEE DataPort): CGAN Model1 achieved 95.19% accuracy11111111.

  • Efficiency: The models were highly efficient, with training times as low as 1 minute and 6 seconds for grayscale classification on the Malimg dataset12121212.

  • False Positive Reduction: Results showed a significant reduction in false positives, which is a major goal in modern cybersecurity13131313.

docs.title: Conclusion for Your Project
docs.text:
The authors conclude that GAN-based models are exceptionally effective for handling obfuscated malware and zero-day attacks14. This report directly supports your original idea of using a "fighting" system (GAN) to build a resilient defense that stays ahead of evolving cyber threats15151515.

Note - CGAN can conditionally generate something, but GAN produces random stuff out of the noise

docs.title: Monetary Policy Instruments
docs.text:
Section 4: Monetary Policy Instruments

• Mandatory Tools (Q):

OMO (Open Market Operation): RBI creates supply of money ↔ Govt instruments (securities sold to get money) (Absorbing and injecting liquidity into the market).

Bank Rate: 6.5% → 10% (Long term - no collateral). Interest at which banks take money from RBI

CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio): (4.5%) A certain percentage of demand and time deposits must be kept with RBI (For controlling inflation and money supply)

SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio): Mandatory 18.5% of demand and time deposits kept with RBI as cash, gold, or govt security (Mandatory reserve requirement set by RBI, requiring commercial banks to maintain a minimum percentage of their demand and time deposits in safe, liquid assets like cash, gold and securities)

Acts a buffer for sudden demands

LAM (Liquidity Adjustment Measures): REPO & REVERSE REPO (short term, collateral required)

  • Tool used in monetary policy that allows bank to borrow money from RBI.
  • REPO is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks when there is shortage of money, for short term and with collateral
  • Reverse REPO is the interest rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks, when is there is surplus of liquidity with the bank.

MSF: Marginal Standing Facility

MSS: Market Stability Scheme

• Target Inflation: 4% (w.e.f 2020) - 2026, ± 2%

• MPC (Monetary Policy Committee): RBI Governor, Deputy Governor, 3 nominees of GOI

Asset: Disbursements to people

docs.title: 1. Anticipation: Planning for the Future
docs.text:
The first step in financial management is anticipation, which involves forecasting future financial needs. This includes estimating revenues, expenses, capital requirements, and cash flow. Financial planning, budgeting, and forecasting are core activities in this phase.

Key Activities:

  • Developing annual budgets
  • Conducting financial forecasting
  • Scenario and risk analysis

Objective: To prepare the organization for both expected and unforeseen financial demands, ensuring long-term sustainability.

docs.title: 2. Acquisition: Securing Financial Resources
docs.text:
Once needs are identified, the next step is acquisition—obtaining the funds necessary to meet those needs. This can involve sourcing capital through equity, debt financing, internal profits, or external grants.

Key Activities:

  • Fundraising
  • Securing loans or investments
  • Managing working capital

Objective: To ensure funds are available at the right time and at the most favorable terms.

docs.title: 3. Allocation: Distributing Financial Resources
docs.text:
With funds secured, the next function is allocation. This step focuses on how best to distribute financial resources across various departments, projects, or investments to maximize efficiency and returns.

Key Activities:

  • Capital budgeting
  • Resource prioritization
  • Investment planning

Objective: To align financial resources with strategic priorities for maximum impact and growth.

docs.title: 4. Appropriation: Controlling and Authorizing Spending
docs.text:
Appropriation refers to the authorized use of financial resources. This function ensures that spending stays within budgetary constraints and complies with internal policies and external regulations.

Key Activities:

  • Expense monitoring
  • Internal controls and approvals
  • Budget enforcement

Objective: To promote accountability and avoid overspending or financial mismanagement.

docs.title: 5. Assessment: Evaluating Financial Performance
docs.text:
Finally, assessment involves evaluating the effectiveness of financial activities. This includes reviewing performance, identifying areas of improvement, and ensuring compliance through audits and analysis.

Key Activities:

  • Financial statement analysis
  • Internal and external audits
  • Performance reviews and KPIs

Objective: To drive continuous improvement, ensure transparency, and support informed decision-making.

docs.title: 4. Capital Market and Issuance of Shares
docs.text:
• Capital Market: A market to meet financial requirements for various business activities, industrial activities and the economic development activities from domestic to international sector.
  • Types:
    • Ownership Based Product (SHARES): Primary (New issued money; direct drawing) and Secondary (Already issued shares; b/w buyers and sellers).
    • Primary - New issued money flows from investors to company through IPO
    • Secondary - Already issued shares flows from investor A to investor B
    • Creditorship (Debt Instruments).
  • Rights of Ownership:
    • Right to income
    • Right to manage
    • Limited liability
    • Right to voting
    • Preemptive rights
  • IPO (Initial Public Offering) & FPO (Follow on Public Offer).
    • IPO is a private company’s first-time sale of shares to the public.
    • FPO is s subsequent issuance of shares by a company who’s shares are already publicly traded.

  • Merchant Bank: Org that takes care of consultancy, issue mgmt, capital restructuring, advisory for mergers, underwriters etc.

    • Consultancy
    • Issue management
    • Underwriters

    • Advisory for mergers

    • Requires Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) or RHP Prospectus.

    • Income: Commission, max (2.5%).
    • Categories: C1 (>5 Cr capital), C2 (>2 Cr capital), C3 (>50 L capital), C4 (No specific - only advisory).

!!! tip "DRHP vs RHP" The prospectus is the operating manual of an IPO, informing investors everything about company’s finances, risks, plans etc. DRHP - FIled with SEBI for review, contains all business and financial details but excludes share price and number of shares. RHP - Filed after SEBI gives its observations. It includes everything except the final price.

  • Pricing of Shares: Fixed price, @ Premium (e.g., @ ₹15 for ₹10 par value), @ Discount (Not permitted), or Book Building process (Floor price, Cap price, Cutoff price).

→ Fixed Price Issue - The company and banker set a specific price before the IPO opens. → Book Building Process - - IPO Process Steps: (1) IPO Issue, (2) FPO issue, (3) Offer for sale, (4) Borrow issue, (5) Rights issue, (6) Pvt. placements, (7) Green shoe option, (8) IPO Grading. - Book Building Calculation: A Dutch auction method to find the cutoff price based on bids (e.g., bids at 16, 14, 12, 10). - Offer for sale - The existing major shareholders will sell their personal shares to public - Bonus Issue - A Bonus Issue involves a company giving free additional shares to existing shareholders. The company will convert its premium to these shares. Market prices will decrease - Rights Issue - This is an invitation to existing shareholders to buy additional new shares, at discounted price |Feature|Option A: Buy (Exercise)|Option B: Sell (Renounce)|Option C: Surrender (Ignore)| |---|---|---|---| |Action Taken|Pay 1,000 for 10 shares.|Sell the 10 "Rights" @ 50.|Do nothing.| |Cash Outflow|- 1,000|0|0| |Cash Inflow|0|+ 500|0| |New Share Count|110|100|100| |Share Price|145.45|145.45|145.45| |Portfolio Value|16,000|14,545|14,545| |Net Wealth|16,000 (Value)|15,045 (Value + Cash)|14,545 (Value)|

  • Private Placement - Instead of going ahead with the general public, the company sells a large block of shares to a select group of investors.
  • Green Shoe Option (Over-allotment option) - Sometimes after an IPO, the price can crash due to heavy selling. The company can issue up-to 15% additional shares than originally planned. The underwriter can buy those over-allotted shares when the price falls the IPO price and buy them back if the demand is high.
  • IPO Grading - The IPO have to be graded by credit rating agencies.

docs.title: 5. Special Share and Debt Instruments
docs.text:
• Bonus Issue: Instead of cash, shares are given as a bonus. No money comes to company; No. of shares increases; EPS and Market Price (MP) decrease.
    • It uses the surplus to stabilize market; Equity capitalization increases.
  • Rights Issue: Additional issue to existing shareholders. They can exercise, transfer, or surrender the right (which is then reissued to general public).
  • Green Shoe Policy: Stability act for reasonable pricing. Merchant bank borrows promoter shares when demand is high to increase MP. Extra shares issued should not be > 15% of capital.
  • IPO Grading: Credit rating for the IPO.
  • Preference Shares (PS) vs Equity (EQ):
    • EQ: Owner, No % return, Profit = dividend, Voting, In management, Last preference in liquidation.
    • PS: Owner/Creditor, Fixed % return, Loss = -%, No voting, Not in management, Additional preference just before liquidation.
  • Types of PS: Cumulative vs non-cumulative, Voting & non-voting, Convertible vs non-convertible, Redeemable vs non-redeemable, Participant vs non-participant. -|Type|Key "Power"| |---|---| |Cumulative|Back-dividends must be paid.| |Participating|Gets "Extra" profit after everyone is paid.| |Convertible|Can turn into Equity (Ownership upside).| |Redeemable|Capital is returned after a fixed time.| |Voting|Can vote in General Body meetings (Rare).|
  • Debt Instruments: Debentures and Bonds. Requires credit rating.
    • Types of Debentures: Naked (unsecured), Secured (mortgage), Guaranteed (third party), Registered & Bearer, Redeemable & non-redeemable, Convertible (Fully or partially).
  • Zero Coupon Bonds / Deep Discounted Bonds (DDB): Deeply discounted (e.g., Price ₹500 for ₹2.5 Lakhs Face Value).
  • Rule 72: (72 / interest rate) = years for money to double.
  • Secured Premium Note (SPN): Principal redeemed after a gap (e.g., 4th–7th year) with a redemption premium.

docs.text:

    • Ownership based: ADR (American Depository Receipts) and GDR (Global Depository Receipts).
    • GBM → MB → Indian Bank with international branch → Listing done with NYSE (Roadshow) → US depository (Converting indian shares to USD)
    • Debt based: FCCB (Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds) and ECB (External Commercial Borrowings).
    • Note: American shares of Indian company cannot be transferred to India.
  • Buy Back of Shares: Since 1998; Buy Back Price (BBP) > Market Price (MP).
  • Mutual Funds (MF):
    • Entities: (1) Sponsor, (2) Trust, (3) Mutual fund company (min. 100 Cr net worth).
    • NAV (Net Asset Value) = (Value of assets – Expenditure) / No. of units. Published every day at 4 PM.
    • Classification: Closed-ended (cannot surrender until end), Open-ended (open throughout), Interval funds (time window each year).
    • Schemes: Equity (Large cap > 10,000 Cr, Mid cap 2000–10,000 Cr, Small cap < 2000 Cr) and Debt funds (Overnight, Liquid, GILT/Govt, etc.).

docs.title: 7. Derivatives
docs.text:
• Derivatives: Financial instruments whose value is determined from an underlying asset (commodity, shares, bonds).
  • Options: Exchange contract between an option holder (buyer) and option writer (seller).
    • European Option: Transaction takes place only on the expiration date (followed in India).
    • American Option: Holder can buy any date from date of contract to expiration.
    • Status: ITM (In the Money - favorable), ATM (At the Money - no difference), OTM (Out of Money).
  • SWAP: Exchange of interest rates (e.g., Fixed 10% for LIBOR rate).
  • Forward Contract: Contract b/w buyer (long position) and seller (short position) for a future date with contingent obligations.

  • Futures: Forward contract prepared in the presence of stock exchange through official channel; exchange takes advance amount from both parties to ensure contract is valid.

  • Forwards: Private, customisation contracts to buy/sell at a future date. High risk of the other person backing out.

  • Futures: Standardised "Forwards" traded on an Exchange. Very safe because the exchange guarantees the deal.
  • Options: Gives you the Right but not the Obligation to buy or sell. If the deal is bad, you can just walk away (losing only your premium).
  • Swaps: Private agreements to exchange cash flows (like swapping a fixed interest rate for a floating one).

Credit Rating Agencies - Evaluate the worthiness of corporate and government debentures. SMERA, CRISIL, CARE, etc.

a Mixin is a way to reuse code across multiple classes without using traditional inheritance. (Represents has-capabilities, and cannot have constructors)

mixin Runner {
  void run() {
    print("Running fast!");
  }
}

class Animal {}

class Dog extends Animal with Runner {}

void main() {
  Dog d = Dog();
  d.run();     // Output: Running fast!
}

mixin Flyer {
  void fly() => print('Flying in the sky');
}

mixin Swimmer {
  void swim() => print('Swimming in water');
}

class Duck with Flyer, Swimmer {}

void main() {
  Duck d = Duck();
  d.fly();
  d.swim();
}

public static void bubbleSort(int[] array) {
    int n = arr.length;
    for(int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for(int j = 0; j < n-i-1; j++) {
            if(arr[j] > arr[j+1]) {
                int temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j+1];
                arr[j+1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Decision Trees
docs.text: A decision tree is a model composed of a collection of "questions" organized hierarchically in the shape of a tree. The questions are usually called a condition, a split, or a test.

docs.title: Axis Aligned vs. Oblique conditions
docs.text:
An axis-aligned condition involves only a single feature. An oblique condition involves multiple features. For example, the following is an axis-aligned condition:

num_legs ≥ 2

num_legs ≥ num_fingers

docs.title: Binary vs. non-binary conditions
docs.text:
Conditions with two possible outcomes (for example, true or false) are called binary conditions. Decision trees containing only binary conditions are called binary decision trees.

Non-binary conditions have more than two possible outcomes. Therefore, non-binary conditions have more discriminative power than binary conditions. Decisions containing one or more non-binary conditions are called non-binary decision trees.

docs.title: Growing Decision Trees
docs.text:
The optimal training of a decision tree is an NP-hard problem.

def train_decision_tree(training_examples):
  root = create_root() # Create a decision tree with a single empty root.
  grow_tree(root, training_examples) # Grow the root node.
  return root

def grow_tree(node, examples):
  condition = find_best_condition(examples) # Find the best condition.

  if condition is None:
    # No satisfying conditions were found, therefore the grow of the branch stops.
    set_leaf_prediction(node, examples)
    return

  # Create two childrens for the node.
  positive_child, negative_child = split_node(node, condition)

  # List the training examples used by each children.
  negative_examples = [example for example in examples if not condition(example)]
  positive_examples = [example for example in examples if condition(example)]

  # Continue the growth of the children.
  grow_tree(negative_child, negative_examples)
  grow_tree(positive_child, positive_examples)

The routine responsible for finding the best conditions is called the splitter.

The score maximised the splitter depends on the task - Information Gain or Gini - Mean squared error is commonly used for regression

docs.title: Binary Classification
docs.text:
Shannon entropy is a measure of disorder

  • Shannon entropy is at a maximum when the labels in the examples are balanced (50% blue and 50% orange).
  • Shannon entropy is at a minimum (value zero) when the labels in the examples are pure (100% blue or 100% orange)

We want to find a condition that decreases the weighted sum of he entropy of the label distributions in T and F. The corresponding score is the information gain

To show you how the formula from developers.google.com works in practice, let's calculate the Information Gain (IG) for a specific split.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: Imagine you have a dataset $D$ of 10 files (5 Malware, 5 Benign). We want to test a split based on a PE feature, such as SizeOfRawData > 500.

docs.title: 1. Calculate Initial Entropy: $H(D)$
docs.text:
The formula for entropy is $H(X) = -p \log p - (1-p) \log (1-p)$, where $p$ is the ratio of the positive label.

  • $p = 5/10 = 0.5$

  • $H(D) = -(0.5 \log_2 0.5) - (0.5 \log_2 0.5) = \mathbf{1.0}$

docs.title: 2. The Split results in $T$ and $F$
docs.text:
Suppose the split SizeOfRawData > 500 divides the files like this:

  • Set $T$ (True): 4 files (4 Malware, 0 Benign)

  • Set $F$ (False): 6 files (1 Malware, 5 Benign)

docs.title: 3. Calculate Entropy for Child Sets: $H(T)$ and $H(F)$
docs.text:
• For Set $T$: $p = 4/4 = 1.0$.

    • $H(T) = -(1 \log 1) - (0 \log 0) = \mathbf{0}$ (This set is perfectly "pure").

  • For Set $F$: $p = 1/6 \approx 0.166$.

    • $H(F) = -(0.166 \log_2 0.166) - (0.834 \log_2 0.834) \approx \mathbf{0.65}$.

docs.title: How data is transported
docs.text:
• Application Layer (Layer 7): This is where your data originates. When you use an application like a web browser to send a request (e.g., typing a URL), the application creates the raw data. This data is then handed down to the layers below.

  • Transport Layer (Layer 4): The data from the application layer is broken down into smaller pieces called segments (if using TCP) or datagrams (if using UDP). The transport layer adds a header containing port numbers for the source and destination application, which allows the data to be delivered to the correct program on the receiving computer. It also includes information for error checking and flow control.

  • Network Layer (Layer 3): The segments or datagrams are now encapsulated into packets. This layer adds an IP header that contains the source and destination IP addresses. This is the crucial information that a router uses to determine the best path for the packet to travel across different networks.

  • Data Link Layer (Layer 2): The packets are then encapsulated into frames. The data link layer adds a MAC address header and a trailer. The MAC addresses are the physical addresses of devices on the same local network (LAN). The header contains the MAC address of the sender (your device) and the MAC address of the next-hop device, which in this case is your router. The trailer contains an error-checking sequence.

  • Physical Layer (Layer 1): Finally, the frame is converted into a stream of raw bits (electrical signals, light pulses, or radio waves) and sent across the physical medium (e.g., Ethernet cable, Wi-Fi).

RIP v1 RIP v2 RIPng Sends update as broadcast Sends update as multicast Sends update as multicast Broadcast at 255.255.255.255 Multicast at 224.0.0.9 Multicast at FF02::9 (RIPng can only run on IPv6 networks) Doesn't support the authentication of updated messages Supports authentication of RIPv2 update messages - Classful routing protocol Classless protocol updated supports classful Classless updates are sent RIP v1 is Classful Routing Protocol - It doesnt send information of subnet mask RIP v2 is Classless Routing Protocol - It sends information of subnet mask in each update
