docs.title: Association
docs.text: An association represents a bi-directional relationship between two classes. It indicates that instances of one class are connected to instances of another class. Associations are typically depicted as a solid line connecting the classes, with optional arrows indicating the direction of the relationship.

docs.title: Dependency

Relationship where one class utilises the services of another class.

        System.out.println(doc.getContent());

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
• Allows to create a new class after extending an existing class
  • Represents Generalization-Specialization relationship
  • Allows overriding existing methods

docs.title: Discriminator
docs.text: Allows one to group subclasses into clusters based on roles

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Leads to tight coupling
  • Indiscriminate use leads to poor quality

docs.title: Iterative and Recursive DNS
docs.text:
In a recursive query, the DNS server does all the work on the behalf of the client. Client sends the query to the DNS, performs a series of iterative queries to other DNS servers to find the answer.

In an iterative query, client asks a root server for the location, returns the address for other server who can resolve the ip address.

  • One master server which holds the original zone file.
  • One slave server which copies zone data automatically from master via zone transfer (AXFR)
. (root)
 └── in
     └── ac
         └── nitc
             └── cse
                 └── nwlab
  • Our DNS servers are authoritative for it.

docs.title: Zone
docs.text: A zone is a portion of DNS namespace that your DNS is authoritative for (trusted). Directory of domain names and their IPs that the DNS server manages.

docs.title: Zone Files
docs.text:
A zone file is a text file that defines all DNS records for a specific domain (zone).

It lives on the master server and is replicated to slaves through zone transfers (AXFR).

/etc/bind/db.nwlab.cse.nitc.ac.in
/var/cache/bind/nwlab.cse.nitc.ac.in

docs.title: Anatomy of a zone file
docs.text:
• SOA - Start of Authority - Declares this server as an authoritative for the zone
  • NS - List of authoritative name servers
  • A - Maps hostname to IPV4
  • AAAA - Maps hostname to IPV6
  • TTL is how long other DNS servers (resolvers or caches) should keep this information before asking again.

!!! tip "Important" Serial number of the zone file must be incremented everytime so that slaves can detect the changes.

  • Refresh - How often the slaves asks for any changes (Serial changes).
  • Retry - Retry time if master not reachable.
  • Expire - Time after which slave discards the data if master is unreachable.
  • Minimum TTL - How long other servers can cache negative responses
| host label | TTL | Class | Record Type | Record data

docs.title: Anatomy of a Zone File
docs.text:
$ORIGIN origin
@ IN SOA {primary-name-server} {hostname-email} (
    {serial-number}
    {time-to-refresh}
    {time-to-retry}
    {time-to-expire}
    {minimum-TTL-for-negative-cache}
)

mail IN A 192.168.1.25
mail IN AAAA fd12:34ab:cdef::101

@ IN MX 10 mail.nwlab.cse.nitc.ac.in

When someone queries DNS for:

  • The query goes to the authoritative servers listed in you NS records.
  • Those servers read the zone file.
  • They return the IP from A record.
  • The client's local resolver caches this for TTL.

docs.title: How Zone Transfers occur
docs.text:
• Slave keeps a copy of the zone and its last-known serial number.
  • Every refresh seconds, it queries the master.
  • AXFR - TCP based operation, sends everything about the zone (authoritative zone transfer)
  • IXFR - More efficient, slave tells the master its current serial number, master checks its change history, if diffs, sends the updated records. (incremental zone transfer)

docs.title: NITCBase
docs.text:
RDBMS implementation project

We are given a Frontend Interface and XFS Interface interacting with the disk

XFS interface - fdisk, print B+ tree, import filename, dump relational catalog, dump attribute catalog, interacting with the file

Frontend Interface - create, drop, open, close, drop index, create index, insert, select, join and select from table where

8 Layer Architecture

Frontend Interface Layer
Physical Layer
Block Access Layer
Buffer Layer
Cache Layer
Schema Layer
Algebra Layer
B+ Tree

Schema Layer - All DDL commands of NITCbase - creating, deleting, opening, closing, renaming attributes and so on.

docs.title:
Create Relation
Delete Relation
Rename Relation 
Rename Attribute 
Create Index
Delete Index
Open Relation
Close Relation
docs.text:
Algebra Layer - All DML commands - Insert, Select, Project, Join

Insert
Project
Select
Join

========================================

Cache Layer - Relation and attribute cache metadata.

Almost all operations on a relation require access to its corresponding Relation Catalog and Attribute Catalog. To prevent multiple reads and writes, Cache Layer caches the catalog blocks, maximum 12 relations can be cached at a time.

struct RelCacheEntry {
    RelCatEntry relCatEntry;
    bool dirty;
    RecId recId;
    RecId searchIndex;
} RelCacheEntry;


struct AttrCacheEntry {
    AttrCatEntry attrCatEntry;
    bool dirty;
    RecId recId;
    IndexId searchIndex;
    struct AttrCacheEntry *next
};
Block Access Layer - Implementation of fundamental DML operations - select and project.

========================================

B+ Layer - Handles indexing operations with B+ trees.

To prevent exhaustive search, m-way search trees -> balanced.

B and B+ Trees are self balanced m way search trees.

B+ Tree -> more number of keys in internal nodes, leaf has all keys appearing. Searching is faster as leaf nodes has a linked list, B Tree would require you to traverse thru every node

========================================

Buffer Layer - Repeated Reads and Writes can be tedious, so NITCBase Maintains a disk buffer that can cache upto 32 disk blocks at a time. The layer contains several access functions that help the higher layer to access the disk at a time.

Buffer replacement handled using LRU scheme.

struct HeadInfo {
    int32_t blockType;
    int32_t pblock;
    int32_t lblock;
    int32_t rblock;
    int32_t numEntries;
    int32_t numAttrs;
    int32_t numSlots;
    unsigned char reserved[4];
};

union Attribute {
    double nVal;
    char sVal[ATTR_SIZE];
};

Buffer Layer has a metadata to store the information regarding the stored disk blocks (free, dirty, timestamp) etc.

Dirty blocks are written back during LRU replacement

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
eBPF is a technology which enables users to extend the functionality of operating systems in a fast and secure way.

eBPF programs can be attached at different points in the kernel and will be called like a function. Programs get called with a context which is a struct with information the kernel is making easily available to the program. Typical examples are a socket buffer or CPU registers.

Program like functions also have return values, the meaning of which is again determined by the return type.

eBPF program are typically written in C and compiled with LLVM.

eBPF programs are loaded into the kernel using BPF syscall, the userspace program that does this is referred to as a loader. When the loader loads a program the kernel will verify that the program is safe.

docs.title: Helper Functions
docs.text: The programs can interact with rest of kernel module using helper functions. These helper functions take upto 5 arguments and return a single return value.

docs.title: KFuncs
docs.text: Instead of creating a special "eBPF-only" function, the kernel developers simply "annotate" existing kernel functions to make them visible to eBPF. This allows eBPF to access a much wider range of kernel features without the overhead of maintaining a separate API.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
#include <linux/bpf.h>
#include <linux/if_ether.h>
#include <linux/ip.h>
#include <linux/udp.h>
#include <bpf/bpf_helpers.h>

SEC("xdp")
int dns_mitigation(struct xdp_md *ctx) {
    void *data_end = (void *)(long)ctx->data_end;
    void *data = (void *)(long)ctx->data;

    // Everything starts with a pointer to the Ethernet header
    struct ethhdr *eth = data;
    // Before reading the Ethernet header, we MUST prove it fits in the packet
    if ((void *)(eth + 1) > data_end)
                return XDP_PASS;

docs.title: Step-by-Step Packet Diving
docs.text:
1. Check for IPv4: Ensure eth->h_proto == htons(ETH_P_IP).

  2. Jump to IP Header: struct iphdr *iph = data + sizeof(struct ethhdr);.

  3. Check for UDP: Ensure iph->protocol == IPPROTO_UDP.

  4. Jump to UDP Header: struct udphdr *udp = (void *)iph + (iph->ihl * 4);.

  5. Check for Port 53: if (ntohs(udp->dest) != 53) return XDP_PASS;.

  6. Find DNS ID: The DNS Transaction ID is the first 2 bytes after the UDP header

docs.title: What happens when a network packet reaches the NIC
docs.text:
When the network packet reaches the NIC, the following happens:

  • When a network packet arrives at the server’s Network Interface Card (NIC), it is first processed by the NIC’s hardware logic. This includes layer-2 framing validation, MAC address filtering, and possibly early classification (such as RSS hash or VLAN tagging). Once the packet is deemed valid and destined for the host, the NIC places the packet into a pre-allocated DMA-capable buffer in host memory location pointed by the receive descriptor ring.
  • To notify the host of new packet arrival, the NIC triggers an Interrupt Request (IRQ). These interrupts signal the CPU to invoke the appropriate kernel driver routine to begin packet processing as shown in the diagram below

  • Once the interrupt is acknowledged, the Linux kernel’s networking stack takes over. It processes packets in a multi-layered pipeline:

  • Data Link Layer: Validates Ethernet frame structure and MAC headers.

  • Network Layer: Handles IP header parsing, routing decisions, and fragmentation (if necessary).
  • Transport Layer: Manages TCP/UDP headers, sequence numbers, port mapping, and flow control.

Packets that successfully pass through the kernel stack are stored in per-socket receive queues, usually called socket buffers (skb). User-space applications retrieve this data using system calls such as recv(), read(), or poll().

  • In blocking mode, the application is put to sleep until data arrives.
  • In non-blocking mode, the call returns immediately if no data is available.

The socket buffer acts as a staging area between the asynchronous kernel processing and application-level consumption.

eBPF sits directly within the Linux kernel, acting as a programmable layer that attaches to hooks at the earliest stages of the networking stack—specifically at the network driver level (XDP) or immediately after Traffic Control. This allows packets to be dropped, redirected, or modified before traversing the full networking stack, offering high-performance networking, security, and observability. 

Key Networking Hook Points:

  • eXpress Data Path (XDP): The lowest-level hook, located directly at the NIC driver upon packet arrival, enabling maximum performance by processing packets before the kernel allocates resources (skb).
  • Traffic Control (TC) Ingress/Egress: Sits within the kernel's TC layer, allowing eBPF programs to inspect, filter, or redirect traffic as it enters or leaves the networking stack.
  • Socket Level (cgroups): Can hook into socket creation to manage networking policies for specific containerized applications.
